speechtext:

subtopic: PORT ARTHUR AND FORT WILLIAM-GOVERNMENT ELEVATORS.
speechtext:
1.	The Government is not aware of any general dissatisfaction with regard to the weights given by the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur.

checked. The Board of Grain Commissioners has on file a statement from one of the largest shippers of grain from Western Canada to the Head of the Lakes, that the outturns of their cars at terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur are 100 per cent satisfactory.

The only thing in the nature of a general complaint received by the Board of Grain Commissioners is that raised by the Order of Grain Buyers; which was fully investigated by the board in January last, and their full report on which is now in the hands of the Government. He said: On the 29th day of last month the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) introduced a resolution in this House which read:	-
That, in the opinion of this House, it is essential for the future national welfare of Canada that appropriate measures be taken by the Government to fit and prepare all immigrants of alien origin for assuming the duties and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship.
That motion was agreed to by the Government and by all hon. members in this House, and in view of that I think I am justified in the assertion that this House acknowledges the existence in Canada of

an undesirable condition of affairs, for the removal of which they suggest that " appropriate measures '' be taken. It is my duty this afternoon to state what I consider to be appropriate measures for satisfactorily coping with this undesirable condition of things, and I trust that hon. members, especially those gentlemen who come from western provinces, will avail themselves of this opportunity to-day to give us the benefit of their observation and experience of conditions as they have found them in Canada, and 'to make suggestions as to how those conditions may be improved. I think we may all take it for granted that it is the common desire of the people of this country to attain, as far as it is possible to do so, some degree of national unity. I think it is a safe assumption that this is the desire of us all. Mr. Speaker, while I hold very strongly to the opinion that the greatest obstacle to national unity, national peace, and national harmony in Canada has been and is that section of the British North America Act which gives complete and exclusive authority to the provinces to deal with educational affairs. I wish to assure the House, notwithstanding that unshake-able opinion, that the resolution which I now propose for consideration is not intended in any sense to infringe upon the rights of the provinces to control their own affairs in the matter of education.
But, Sir, while it is not my intention to make any motion that will tend to encroach upon the constitutional rights of the provinces to control their own educational systems, I do believe that this House can, and I say now that it should, take some definite steps at the earliest possible moment to assist the provinces in the important and far-reaching task of developing a class of citizens who will not only understand and fully appreciate the duties and responsibilities of high Canadian citizenship, but who will be as ready to bear their full share of those duties and responsibilities as they are anxious to participate in all the benefits and privileges of citizenship within the borders of Canada. We have aided the provinces in many ways by grants of money, and otherwise, in respect to matters which were just as strictly provincial and just as entirely within the jurisdiction of the Provincial Parliaments, as is this matter of education. I am free to admit, Mr. Speaker, that the provinces have done a great deal in the direction of educating the people and in developing their own educational systems. But I also believe that we have ample evidence that the provinces have
failed to produce the kind of citizens whom we should desire to see in Canada. I make this statement as applicable in a general sense. They have failed because there are in every province a deplorable number of illiterates; and, to this extent at any rate, I think I may say without fear of contradiction that the provinces have failed in their duty to develop a proper Canadian citizenship. Their task, I grant, has been difficult, and a good part of the burden which the provinces have had to bear in the matter of education has been placed upon their shoulders by the Government at Ottawa. In order to show the true condition of educational affairs in Canada and, at the same time, to emphasize as briefly and as clearly as I possibly can the necessity for supplementing the work that has been carried on by the provinces, I purpose to give a few figures to the House. These figures I am taking from the official census records of 1911. Of our population in 1911, five years of age and over, 663,453 were unable to read or write any language, or 105 out of each 1,000 of the population. In 1901 143 out of each 1,000 of the population were unable to read or write any language. These figures indicate that some improvement has been made in the interval, and I wish to give the provinces credit for it. In regard to these illiterates to whom I have called your attention it may be of interest to note that ,115 males and 98 females in each 1,000 were born in Canada, that 38 males and 41 females were British, born outside Canada, and that 169 males and 170 females were foreign born.
But I want to speak more particularly this afternoon of the illiterates, 21 years and over-that is illiterates of voting age-those who, because of their age, are recognized as having the right to select their representatives in this Parliament and in the provincial parliaments. I think that from what I have said we have very litle ground to complain of illiteracy on the part of British immigrants coming into this country. Indeed, so long as the number of Canadian born illiterates is about three to one of the British born, it ill becomes us to criticise, on the ground of their illiteracy, the immigrants coming from other parts of the British Empire.
The large number of Canadian born illiterates demonstrates, to my mind, the inefficiency of the various provincial departments of education in handling their educational problems, and also the need of this Government coming to the assistance of the

provinces in that work. I am sure you will all agree with me when I say that at least all Canadian and British born citizens should be able to read and write and take an intelligent interest in public affairs, and should be able to assist in the task of Canadianizing those who come from foreign lands. Unfortunately we have thousands of Canadians, thousands of citizens born in Canada, who are almost as alien as those who come to this country from foreign lands and who are in no better position to shoulder their share of the responsibilities of Canadian citizenship than are those who' may be denominated as foreigners.
Let us consider in this connection the problems which the province of Saskatchewan has to face, and in referring particularly to that province I will be indicating very similar conditions in the other three western provinces and to some extent conditions which are similar in the older provinces in the East. From a report which I have here which is entitled "Saskatchewan Educational Survey," and which was prepared at the instance of the Saskatchewan Government and submitted to the public with their approval and sanction, I find that out of 2,100 rural schools in that province there were 150 Slavonic schools. What I wish particularly to direct your attention to is that in these 150 Slavonic schools there were 4,806 pupils in all grades.' Of those pupils 2,577 were in grade one; that is to say those just beginning at the age of six years.

Are you now referring to
the year 1911?	.

No. I thank the hon. gentleman for that question. This report refers to the year 1916. I wish you to know that in the second grade there were only'692 pupils; in the fifth grade -that would be from ten years on-there were 183 and when we reach the eighth grade -that is 13 years and over-the number drops to 39. It must be apparent to every person that in the cases I have mentioned nearly all of these children left school without any knowledge of Canadian history and without any appreciation of, or training in, the essentials of Canadian citizenship.
There were in the province of Saskatchewan, in 1916, according to this report, 18,934 Mennonites. It is a well known fact that these Mennonites have persistently resisted all attempts to organize public schools or to be instructed in English. They have assumed an attitude of hostility along these lines ever since they came into the 
country. Who is to blame? Are we to place the blame for that on the Saskatchewan Government? I do not think so. The reason I do not think so is because of an agreement which was entered into between the Mennonites and the Federal Government of Canada in July 1873, by which agreement the Mennonites were exempted from military service. But I will quote the words of that agreement, showing that there was another exemption. Those words are:
The fullest privilege of exercising their religious principles as by law afforded the Mennonites without any kind of niclestation or restriction whatever, anjl the same privilege extends to the education of their children in the schools.
That was an exemption or privilege-call it what you like-which was placed in that agreement. They were so eager to get these people into the country that the Government of that day entered into an agreement which, to say the least of it, was in my opinion an extremely foolish agreement. The Parliament which passed a law of that kind should not shirk its duty now in shouldering a part of the burden which it, by that law, imposed upon the province of Saskatchewan and upon the Dominion of Canada. Then there are, according to the report, in addition to these Mennonites, 5,880 Douk-hobours with their community schools conducted in the German language; about 78,428 people of Russian, and Austro-iHungar-ian origin and 27,506 Ruthenians of different kinds, or a total of 130,748, of those whom I have mentioned.
Now, Sir, when we realize the fact that about 60 per cent of those that I have named get no further than grade 1, we can understand, that we are turning out in that country, year after year, a class of citizens who have not the faintest conception of the duties of Canadian 'citizenship, or any appreciation of what they owe to this country. Nearly one-half of the population of Saskatchewan is of foreign birth; and I think that there were over 100,000 in the three Prairie Provinces in 1916 who could not speak a word of English. Under those conditions, Mr. Speaker, can you wonder that the report from which I have quoted, and which I say was issued with the approval of the Saskatchewan Government, contains this recommendation:
That the Dominion Government he urged to pass the necessary legislation to provide a fund for the elimination of adult illiteracy, to be distributed among the several provinces for evening schools and continuation schools.
There you have an expression of opinion from the province of Saskatchewan; and if

I had no other warrant for proposing the present resolution, Jthat recommendation from the Saskatchewan Government, I think, would be sufficient to justify me in asking your earnest consideration of this matter.
Sir, we have in Canada, some fifty odd different nationalities, speaking some eighty different languages and dialects. Between forty and fifty per cent of the .population of Canada west of the Great Lakes is not Anglo-Saxon. These different races and groups are estimating this country and its institutions, and their duties and responsibilities as citizens, from fifty different viewpoints. The task which lies before us as members of this House, as (well as before the various provincial legislatures, is to, as speedily as possible, reduce those fifty different viewpoints to one viewpoint, and that the Canadian viewpoint. In this connection I would like to quote from an address which was delivered in the city of Winnipeg last October by T)r. Anderson of Regina, Saskatchewan. I may say that the occasion on which Dr. Anderson delivered this address was the holding of a great educational conference in that city, a conference which was called "The National Conference on character .education in relation to Canadian Citizenship." There were at that conference, which lasted three days, .some 1,500 accredited delegates from every province of the Dominion. There were also present as delegates, leading educationists from the United States, and from the United Kingdom. I believe I am right in saying that every province in Canada was represented at that conference; I think I am right in saying that every university in Canada was represented; and I am sure I am right in saying that that conference was the largest educational conference ever held in this Dominion, and one of the largest of ,the kind ever held on the North American continent. That alone is sufficient to indicate that those who are spending their lives in, and devoting all their energies and abilities to educational matters showed *their keen interest by travelling some of them hundreds and others thousands of miles at their own expense to attend that conference, talk over matters relating to this Dominion, and confer together as to the weaknesses in our national system and endeavour to arrive at some conclusion as to how those weaknesses might be remedied. The gentleman to -whom I refer, Dr. Anderson, is the "Director of Education among the hewer Canadians" in the province of
iSaskatchewan. In the course of Ms address, after referring to the large immigration into this country, Dr. Anderson says:
As the result of this tremendous human influx from practically all over the face of the earth, we have in Canada to-day large areas, urban as well as rural, populated with unassimilated groups with varying _ social ideals, varying languages, and varying ideas of Canadian citizenship and loyalty to the British Empire. This situation has been with us for years, but we have neglected to face it with any definite national policy. I say a " definite national policy," with a full realization of the fact that each province has the right-the sole right-to deal with its own peculiar educational problems. But this problem of citizenship is one that vitally affects this young nation, and I see no reason why a fairly uniform system in dealing with the question of racial assimilation should not be universally adopted throughout our Dominion. At any rate, we shall never obtain a satisfactory solution until every province realizes to the full that from an educational standpoint at least it must regard great public questions from a national as well as from a provincial point of view. Just so long as it is necessary to conduct public meetings, to write hooks and publish newspapers and magazines in a dozen foreign languages, just so long as this undesirable condition in our public affairs exists, we cannot hope for national unity throughout this fair Dominion.
Mr. Speaker, may I refer, just for a, (moment, to the .matter of history to emphasize what has been said? I wonder sometimes if we really appreciate the fact that we live in a country of such vast extent that it -contains provinces as large as many independent countries in the world.
.1 wonder sometimes if we really appreciate what that means in our coming together; or, if you like to put it the other way, what that means in having a tendency to separate. Now what do we find? Starting at the Atlantic ocean and taking province by province you will find that we have in the nine different provinces nine different kinds of history taught. And yet we are looking forward to this becoming a united country whose people will understand history, especially Canadian history from the same *standpoint. I think that such a condition does not make foe,unity; I believe it makes for disunity.	_
Now I am not suggesting that this Federal Board of Education should enforce the teaching of one kind of history-I believe history is not history unless it is a record of facts, I do not say that the Federal Bureau .should take upon itself to say what kind of history should be taught in the various provinces; but I do believe this-and I am confirmed in my belief after carefully reading what took place at the three days' conference in Winnipeg-that

there is sufficient breadth of view amongst the men who direct our educational affairs in the several provinces to enable them to come together and discuss, we will say, matters in relation to history and perhaps form a united opinion as to what kind of history it will be best to authorize. But let me repeat once more that I have no desire, and I think it would be very inadvisable to attempt to compel the provinces to depart from what their own educationalists might think was the proper course to take in regard to teaching history or any other subject. We also, if we are to succeed in the stupendous task of Canadianization, must be dominated by one lofty ideal of Canadian national unity resting on the firm basis of devoted and intelligent citizenship. We must be fired by this dominating ideal if we are to succeed. I trust that as a result of this great national conference steps will be taken leading to the establishment of a Dominion Bureau of Education which will he a co-operating, vitalizing and inspiring factor in building up a strong unified Canadian nation.
It seems to me, Sir, that we cannot very well expect unity or concerted action so long as we have various groups in this Dominion clinging to the systems and ideals that they have brought with them from their native countries in Europe. I think, Sir, that this Parliament has not only the right to take definite action, but I believe it is its bounden duty to move in the matter. In that connection may I ask the House to consider this point. The late war disclosed Canada's strength. We are very apt to dwell on that feature; but it is just as true that that war also disclosed Canada's weakness, for it showed that there were thousands of people in this country

enjoying all the privileges of Canadian citizenship who were not prepared to bear their share of the burden of responsibility of that citizenship, and we realized that when a national crisis arose we could not depend on them to perform their part as patriotic citizens. I am not attempting to place the blame for that state of affairs, I am merely stating a fact that I think no one will question. That being so, I think it is indisputable that the responsibility for concerted war action rested-not upon the , several provinces, but upon the Federal Parliament; that was the authority we looked to to see that Canada did its whole duty in that war.
And yet in those things which make for the unifying of a people through the constitutional right of Parliament to interfere in educational matters, the Dominion Parliament has absolutely no authority whatever to check or prevent the inculcation of false ideals or the dissemination of false doctrines throughout this country. This Parliament was held responsible for Canada doing its full share in the war. Every person will agree on the importance of education in bringing people to that frame of mind where they will be willing "to do their bit," yet in matters of such vital importance as education this Parliament has absolutely no constitutional right to interfere in any shape or form.
Now, Sir, I am not advocating that we should put forward any claim to interfere with the rights of the provinces. I know the provinces are jealous of those rights, and I do not want this Parliament to infringe upon them; but I do believe it is possible for the Dominion to co-operate with the provinces in matters of education without in the slightest degree infringing upon provincial rights. Indeed, by co-operation I think we can give the provinces very valuable assistance.
Talking about our rights as a Parliament to check those influences which disunite our people, why, it was admitted in this House only a few days ago by the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster) that we have no machinery for stopping the circulation in Canada of those infamous publications known as the Hearst papers. Well, it seems to me that it is pretty nearly time we devised the necessary machinery to deal with that sort of thingf.

Mr. Speaker, the facts which I have placed (before the House demonstrate the need for (assistance to the provinces in the matter of education. I now come to the proposal which I have to offer, namely, the establishment in Ottawa of a Federal Bureau of (Education.
* The idea of a Federal Bureau of Education is not a new one; leading educationists have advocated it for a great many years.
In the United States they have had a Federal Bureau of Education for fifty-two or fifty-three years. The various States on the other side of the line have control over their own educational affairs, and never during the whole fifty years the Federal Bureau of Education Jias been in existence has it attempted to infringe on the rights of the States in any respect. There has been no complaint whatever along that line. On the contrary, the good work which has been done by the United States Federal Bureau has been so widely recognized all over the United States that at the present time there is a very strong demand to raise

it from the status of a bureau to that of a department.
I referred a few moments ago to a speech delivered by Dr. Anderson at the Educational Conference in the city of. Winnipeg. On the third day of the Conference a resolution was moved, and I shall give its wording because it indicates some of the work which I think should be undertaken by the Federal Government. It is as follows :
That this National Conference on Character Education express its approval of the organization of a Dominion Bureau of Education, whose duties shall be to oolleot such statistics and facts and general information as Shall show the condition and progress of education in the several provinces and territories, and to diffuse such information respecting the organization and management of school systems and methods of teaching, as shall aid the people of Canada in the establishment and maintenance of efficient school systems, and otherwise promote the cause of education throughout the country.
That resolution was spoken to by many gentlemen, and I shall quote a few opinions. Professor Coleman, of Queen's University, said:	-
A Bureau of Education in the United States, established years ago, has done a wonderful work in that country. A great need exists for a similar work to he done in our own country.
Dr. Bexford, of (Montreal, said:
The resolution as I may say for your information, is a resolution similar to that which incorporated the United States Bureau of Education fifty-two years ago, and we know something of what that Bureau has been to the cause of education in the United States. Are we not ready to begin something of a national character in this country?
Dr. Milton Fairchild, who is Chairman of the Executive Committee of the National Institution for Moral Instruction, Washington, D.C., spoke as follows:
I do not want to discuss your problems, but 1 would like to clear up some misunderstandings in regard to our Bureau of Education. It now and then makes a survey on request from a State, of the education going on in the State, carrying to the survey the information which the experts of the bureau have. It is also true that in the new Bill for the establishment of a Department of Education, no supervisory powers are given to the new Department of Education, but all control and all decisions rest in the States, with the State Department of Education and the State government.
Professor Coleman also said:
I am a professor of education in one of our Eastern universities, and my business is to train high school teachers, inspectors, and, presumably, leaders in education. All our up-to-date

information practically comes to us from the United States. We use the Bulletins of the United States Bureau of Education, to know what is going on in the Western Provinces
even	The most effective way,
because it promises the most permanence, and will assure us less bias, or. less chance pf being accused of bias, the most effective way of carrying out our purpose, is by a Bureau of Education, which will not in any way infringe upon or impair provincial rights.
Was that resolution adopted unanimously at the Winnipeg Conference?

No, the resolution was not adopted. It was debated in the afternoon of the third day, and it was decided to leave the matter over until the evening. At the evening session an amendment *was moved to the effect that instead of having a Federal Bureau at Ottawa there should be a bureau appointed by the Conference for doing what I have suggested is the proper work of a Federal Bureau at Ottawa, and the Conference proceeded to act upon that suggestion. A cojmcil of fifty was appointed. Four were chosen from each of the nine provinces and these thirty-six chose the other fourteen. This council is a sort of national organization of fifty created for the purpose of carrying on, as far as it could, the work that is now being done by the Federal Bureau in the United States. There seemed to be a fear, ungrounded, I think, on the part of some present-at the 'Conference that a Federal Bureau at Ottawa would in some way interfere with provincial rights and provincial control over educational matters. The Conference was the first of its kind ever held in the Dominion and there was a disposition amongst all the delegates from all the provinces that the cordial feelings which had existed throughout the three days should not be impaired by any dissension at the close, and some of those who had spoken very strongly in favour of a Federal Bureau of Education therefor accepted the compromise, because they did not feel it would be wise to have it go out that there was any very strong difference of opinion in the closing hours of the Conference.
While that was the position taken by the Conference at Winnipeg, at all events there was no difference of opinion amongst the fifteen hundred delegates there present in regard to the advisability of such a bureau as I have suggested. There was, however, some difference of opinion as to whether the bureau should be established at Ottawa and maintained by the funds of the Dominion of Canada, or whether it should be established by the persons who form the conference, and carried on by private subscription alone, or, as has been suggested, by private subscription with assistance from this Government. Now, I have presented arguments in support of my contention that this Government should take an active part in this matter, and I think I have proved the necessity for having the bureau established in Ottawa. To make somewhat clearer just what the work of the bureau would be I shall refer for a moment or two to these documents which contain the report of the United States Bureau of Education. This report says:
The bureau is therefore under permanent obligation to assemble periodically statistics bearing upon all phases of educational activity. The collection, tabulation and interpretation of such statistics involve the labour of a considerable
number of persons	The bureau is
approached for information by thousands of citizens of the United States, and by individuals and official agencies from all parts of the world. This information is furnished through the medium of letters and printed documents.
The report goes on to say that in the statistical division, in the year 1917, returns were collected, tabulated and summarized from, 20,759 schools, and reference is made to hundreds of thousands of letters and bulletins which were sent out by that bureau. Attention is drawn, for example, to such matters as the special purposes of these bulletins, agricultural and rural education, teachers' pensions, commercial education, state school systems, and a great many other subjects which I shall not delay the House by reading. That bureau carries on extensive operations that are of great importance. For instance, a certain state requests the bureau to investigate its educational conditions. The bureau undertakes such an investigation, goes into the history of education in that particular state, ascertains the shortcomings of the system which has been in vogue, and makes a report of its findings, and it can be readily seen what an advantage such an investigation must be to those who are engaged in the profession of teaching. There is* a report here in regard to the state of Ohio, one in regard to Colorado, another in regard to the state of New York. ' Those who are interested in matters educational and who desire to see established in any state the very best system which proper management and thorough acquaintance with conditions can devise, have merely to write to the Federal Bureau to obtain the latest reports and such information as will reveal the defects in their own systems by comparison with the methods followed in

other states. Surely we could carry on some such work at Ottawa if there were a Federal Bureau here. I wonder how many hon. members could stand up here this afternoon and give a comprehensive and definite statement in regard to the school system of any province other than their own. I know that I for one could not do so, notwithstanding the fact that I have naturally taken a great interest in educational matters having been engaged in teaching school for a number of years both in this province and in the province of Manitoba. How many members in the provincial legislature of Ontario could explain every detail of the Ontario educational system? Again, how many in Ontario have any idea of the system employed in the province of Quebec? Or how many persons in Quebec can give a fairly accurate description of the system followed in Ontario or in Manitoba? How many in Manitoba know anything about the system in British Columbia? It seems to me to be manifest that if we had a bureau collecting information in regard to the various systems in the provinces each province would be placed in an advantageous position in regard to education, because each would be able to make use of the information so gathered and determine whether its own system, in comparison with those of other provinces, was defective, or, at least, left room for improvement. I shall suggest some things which I think a bureau such as I advocate might take up with advantage. First of all, I think that the first step in the establishment of a Federal Bureau should be an invitation by this Government to the various Provincial Governments to send two or three of their leading' educationists to Ottawa to meet in conference and talk the subject over, and discuss just what the bureau should do. Would it be too much to ask that this Government set aside $1,000,000, and the nine provinces among them set aside another $1,000,000, to be spread over, let us say, five years in developing the school as a community centre and as an instrument for Canadiani-zation?
We can vote millions for the improvement of roads, for technical education, for assistance to the provinces in the matter of agricultural education, and for other purposes. Along many lines we can vote, and we have voted considerable money. But is any one of these projects for which we have voted money and which are as distinctly provincial in their character, so far as jurisdiction at least is concerned, as the matter of education, to be comnared in importance

with the problem of properly educating the people so that they may become worthy citizens of whom we may be proud? This money might be used for the purpose of placing before the people of Canada the advantages of a unifying Canadianization movement with the school as its symbol and centre, and for distributing, especially throughout the non-English schools, attractive and interesting booklets well illustrated, dealing with Canadian ideals, standards of living, methods of government, the history and development of the country, the great leaders and heroes of Canada, etc. It might be used for promoting a community centre movement to bring together the people of all Canadian communities. In this regard allow me to call attention to the fact that in some of the western provinces, where the foreigners have been allowed to settle in groups, they realize just as much as we do the value of the community centre. They recognize the importance and advantages of amicable social intercourse, and they are forming themselves into community centres. These foreigners are getting together into national communities-for what purpose? Sociability is of course one of their objects, but they are getting together more for the purpose of retaining the ideals which they brought with them to this country, and inculcating in their young those ideals rather than the ideals of Canadian citizenship.
Next, I suggest that some of the money might be properly used for the purpose of giving assistance in the formation of night classes, and the preparation of special books suited to these classes. Many of these people, especially the foreign element, as I have shown, do not send their children to school as they should. The children are out of school when still very young.
I believe from what I have read, from what I have gathered and from what I have stated , in this House, that very many of these foreigners out in out , Western Provinces are eager to learn Canadian customs and would be glad to get any information that it is possible for us to give them. I believe from what I have read and from what I have heard that- they would respond to any eff ort in the direction of establishing these night schools, and I think we should make an effort along that line. If we expect that we are going to make Canadian citizens out of these people, if we expect them to bear their share of the burdens of this country when burdens come, we should do what we can to put them in a position to understand Canadian citizenship and the Canadian form of Government.

I think that special encouragement might be given, to school consolidations and continuation classes in accordance with the recommendation I read a moment ago from the province of Saskatchewan. Some assistance might be given along that line. Some special assistance might be given in training teachers especially for those schools where the foreign element predominate. Lectures might be given in various parts of Canada, illustrated with lantern slides and so on, and I have no doubt that a great deal of instruction might be given in that way to these people whom we want to make good Canadian citizens.
"Oh," but some person objects, "that is the work of the provinces." With all due deference to those Who hold that opinion, I wish to say very emphatically that we are not playing the game and playing it fairly, if we place, or continue to allow to be placed, upon the shoulders of the provinces the entire responsibility for Canadianizing the immigrants that we, and not the provinces, bring into this country. This Government owes a duty to the Dominion of Canada and it has not in the past made any attempt to carry out its part in this matter. We are simply shirking the responsibility when we say, "Oh, under section 93 of the British North America Act, that is a matter for the provinces to deal with," and let it go at that. We cannot get rid of our responsibility in that way. We have had ample opportunity to know what the situation is. When we look at the figures we see that the provinces have not been able apparently to deal as effectively with this matter as they should in the interest of Canada. Are we going to fold our arms and say that we have no interest in this matter whatever and let it go at that? I do not think that is the proper attitude to take. We are shirking our responsibility if we take that attitude.
The war taught a great many lessons. I have often heard the statement made that the war was fought to crush ouf militarism and to make the world safe for democracy. It seemed to me that the next thing in the human drama, in which some 66,000 Canadians laid down their lives, is to take the necessary steps to make democracy safe for the world and we cannot fold oiw arms and say : " This is a matter for the provinces to deal with and we have no concern in it." That is not the kind of courage out boys displayed in making the world safe for democracy.
There is a good deal of social unrest all over the world and we find that there have 88
been what you might call " populistic " uprisings in certain	countries.	In theUnited States	and	indeed	in	Canada,we have had	the	shadow	of	the redhand. We have had enough to show us that it is	time	for us	to	make a
move towards getting rid of this illiteracy or ignorance which is a menace to any country. There is any amount of evidence to show that we have in Canada to-day those who would disintegrate and destroy everything that makes for national progress and stability. Their motto appears to be to satisfy the elementary desires with the least effort possible. They would bring all to a dead level if they could and, setting aside all human experiences, life to them would consist of eating, drinking, sleeping and having a good time. They sneer at the success which is only to be obtained by the greatest personal sacrifice and hard labour and they scorn the accumulations of art, science, literature and history. Their only hope for carrying on their propaganda is ignorance and illiteracy amongst certain classes of our population. They know that they have no hope of success with an educated and enlightened people. ' Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I feel we have an obligation resting upon onr shoulders and that this Parliament should do something to assist the provinces to grapple with the problem of Canadianizing especially the foreign ele-.ment. I believe that we can do a great work here, just as great a work as that which has been done by the Federal 'Bureau in the United States. I am sure that work can be done without infringing in the slightest degree upon the authority of the provinces to handle and manage their educational affairs I think it should be done co-operatively. I say that the bureau would not have the right to attempt to, and would not in the slightest degree, infringe upon provincial authority in educational matters. But I cannot help but think that great benefit would accrue to every one of the provinces just in the coming together of their leading educationists and discussing matters of education affecting the whole Dominion of Canada. After all we want a united Canadian citizenship not in one province but in the whole of the nine provinces. I believe that another thing that can be said in favour of this bureau is that it would have a tendency to break down those barriers which to-day to a great extent separate the provinces and make them feel that they must confine their activities to their own particular domains. It would break down those barriers, make for closer union one with the other and result



in very great benefit to the whole of Canada. I have very great pleasure in moving the resolution seconded by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Anderson).

Mr. Speaker, in rising to offer a few remarks on the resolution introduced by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Edwards) I desire to say at the' outset that I do not wish in the least to minimize the paramount importance of public instruction or of education. But I beg to disagree with my hon. friend when he claims that there is a duty devolving upon this Parliament to organize and establish a Federal Bureau of Education which would in a way, exercise a certain amount of authority over the provincial legislatures. That defects in education exist in the different provinces of Canada I believe every hon. member within my hearing will admit; perfection does not belong to this world. But every legislature in Canada, every Provincial Government, is fully aware of those defects; and I believe it is doing those legislatures an injustice to contend that they are not bringing to the task of wiping out these deficiencies the courage, the energy, and the attention that the situation demands.
My hon. friend has rather gloomily pictured the educational .situation of Canada; indeed if I have taken down his words accurately, he characterized that situation as deplorable. He refrained, in particular, from making any allusion to any other province than the province of Saskatchewan. But in that province especially he referred to a situation arising from the presence amongst their inhabitants of a certain religious class; and if I understood the hon. gentleman aright, this particular class was enjoying certain privileges not by reason of the British North America Act, but owing to the fact that certain legislation had been passed by this Parliament. Therefore, the remedy would lie with this Parliament in so far as this particular class of citizens is concerned.
I must confess that my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) presented his case in a dispassionate spirit which is highly commendable and for which I have no hesitation in extending him my congratulations. He has defended himself very strongly from the accusation that could be brought home to him of attempting to infringe upon the rights, or privileges, conferred upon the provinces by the Constitution. I must say immediately, however, that I fear the creation of a Fed-e-'-] Bureau of Education would be construed in the different provinces as an encroachment upon their rights.

My hon. friend, in the course of his remarks, and especially in his concluding observations, made an allusion to the conference held in Winnipeg, at which several resolutions in regard to education were presented, many of which were rejected and a few adopted. He also pointed out that it would be proper that the Federal authorities should grant certain assistance to such an independent educational body as that conference was. To that there cannot be. any objection. That this Government should grant financial aid to those educational authorities to get together annually or biannually in order to discuss between themselves the great educational problems, representatives as they are of every province in the Dominion, cannot be objected to- the collection of information in that way would be useful. But the moment you clothe the Bureau of Education with the Federal authority, then you encroach upon the rights of the provinces as guaranteed by the Constitution.
My hon. friend also referred to one particular feature of the effects that would be obtained by the creation of such a bureau^ He intimated that it would be efficacious in removing a spirit of prejudice and intolerance in 'Canada. There is no doubt that a certain spirit of prejudice and intolerance does exist in Canada. I am, however, of the . opinion expressed at the opening of the present session by the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government for the time being, that these prejudices are fast dying out. As far as the province from which I come is concerned, there is no spirit of intolerance. Strange as the statement may sound in your ears, strange as the affirmation may appear to you, there is, in the province of Quebec, no intolerance. This I could demonstrate by endless and numberless incidents and citations, but I am not going to burden the House with them. I will content myself with saying that as I was about to rise from my seat my eyes fell upon a newspaper on my desk, and which I had not yet had time to read to-day. i now have before me this morning's issue of the Montreal Gazette, and on the last page of that paper you will read a short despatch; professing to be a 'Canadian press cablegram from London. It is dated April 17, and it reads:
Sir Andrew MacPhail, of Montreal, had a letter in yesterday's Spectator, the Londonweekly review, defending Quebec from criticisms made in a hook by Hugh Stutfield, which, he says, may be an honest book, but the instruct tion therein anent Quebec is incorrect in every particular. Sir Andrew asserts that Quebec

people are more tolerant of all kinds of education and religious forms and the least tolerant of fanatism. Quebec is the only place in the [DOT]world, he says, which has successfully withstood the emissaries of evil from the labour world of Europe. Lastly, adds Sir Andrew, the only two churches in Canada, which do not interfere in politics, are the Roman Catholic Church and the Church of Scotland. The Spectator also, as an editorial on the Irish question, which recalls Canada's political troubles in the early part of the last century, which the Spectator submits, contain a warning for those Independent Liberals, who denounce the Home Rule Bill because it faces realities, and admits that Ulster is as profoundly hostile to the south and west of Ireland as Ontario was to Quebec. In Canada, says the journal, it is certain that religious disputes have lost much of their bitterness in the past half century and, reverting to Sir Andrew McPhail's letter, it says that his statement confirms the wisdom of the partition affected in 1867 between Quebec and Ontario.
I could quote much of similar testimony to the like effect, especially from letters addressed to the authorities of Laval university accompanying contributions to the rebuilding fund, but I must not delay the House. The question of education in this country is in a class by itself, and it is so treated in the British North America Act. For instance, it cannot be likened to or assimilated-
