Mr. BELAiND: I thank my hon. friend for the correction. II thought that it must have been a mistake as printed here. Referring to the question of education, Mr. Speaker, it cannot be compared to or assimilated with the question of, for instance, public health. We have been more or less accustomed to regard the latter question as pertaining exclusively to the provinces, though in the British North America Act there is nothing to indicate that public health is left particularly to provincial jurisdiction. One has only to think of the inspection of immigrants; the establishment of quarantine stations, the pollution of interprovincial streams; the examination of animals for slaughter and the preservation of their health in general; the sale, manufacture and importation of food products and of drugs-all of which have a direct bearing upon public health-to realize that they cannot be considered in the same class as education. In their very nature they are matters of federal jurisdiction, at least to a large extent. But the spirit and the letter of the British North America Act 884
confine education to the jurisdiction of the provinces.
Why is it, it may be asked, that the Fathers of Confederation thought it judicious to make that stipulation? No doubt at that time of Confederation there existed -as there exists to-day-a body of opinion which held that neutral or public schools were preferable; but there also existed at that time a large body of opinion which held that religious education must be at the bottom of public instruction. I am not here to discuss in particular the merits or the demerits of public schools as against separate or denominational schools, for I do not think it is pertinent to this discussion. But be that as it may, Confederation itself was a compromise, and the result of that compromise was the consecration of the principle that in some of the provinces separate schools should be maintained; in other words, that the wishes of the parents should be respected in all matters of education. To-day fully one-third of our population holds the same view.
It would be idle, Mr. Speaker, to attempt to assimilate the science of health, for instance, with the science of education. While it is possible in matters of public health, to reach uniformity of views, regardless of creed or of race, and whilst it is possible to enact laws and to pass regulations of general application for its preservation, it is impossible to secure the same unanimity in matters of education, especially of primary education.	-
As I said a few minutes ago, Mr. Speaker, I refrain from entering upon a comparison of both systems of education-the public, or neutral system, as it is generally known, and the religious system. It might lead to the creation of ill-feeling or the accentuation of that ill-feeling. wherever it may now exist. All I want to say is that so far as Canada is concerned-and I know my hon. friend will bear me out-the system which has as its main foundation the teaching of religion, has justified its existence during the last few years. Stability in a social sense as well as a political sense, resistance to the penetration of ultraradical principles, is evidence of the efficacy of religious education in our schools. No doubt, as my hon. friend has very properly contended, instruction has an allimportant role to play, not only in Canada, but in the world.
It has a part to play in the struggle of existence. It has a great part to play in the race for supremacy in commercial and

industrial activities. But while instruction is paramount in importance, can it compare with what may be more properly called education? Instruction is the cultivation *of mind by knowledge. Education is the [DOT]cultivation of the heart; the cultivation in the heart of true and sound principles of family affection; a realization of duty, the practice of religious and moral obligations, and, perhaps above all, respect for authority. All these principles are absolutely important as forming a firm basis of human society.
I do my hon. friend the credit of saying that he is animated by a desire to render service to his country. He wants to develop in this country what he terms a spirit of Canadianism. I share his view entirely. What is patriotism? Patriotism is a deep sense of national honour backed up by love of home and pride of race, sustained and -supported by unalterable attachment to traditions and to institutions. Institutions may be political or they may be religious. Traditions are not the same to all races. An Englishman in Canada may be proud of his ancestors and of their doings in history; they are a part of his domestic domain, as I would call it. It is his tradition; it belongs to him; he is attached to it. The Fiench Canadian is deeply and firmly attached to his religious institutions. In what you call the separate schools the children are imbued with the spirit of the religious institution and have a respect for tradition. As to political in-5 p.m. stitutions, is there a province in Canada where the spirit of preserving our British institutions is not highly cultivated? I am not as conversant with the schools of other provinces as I am with those of Quebec,-my hon. friend has properly said that we can hardly be as conversant with other provinces as we are with our own-but I take it for granted that in all the schools of other provinces the true spirit of Canadianism is highly cultivated and maintained.
My hon. friend is wrong in that..

Well, I can speak more particularly for the province of Quebec. There, tradition is revered; the religious spirit of our ancestors is preserved. The political institutions of Great Britain, as they are implanted in Canada, are just as sacred to French-Canadians as they are to British-Canadians.
Uniformity has its advantages, but so has variety. The visitor who travels
fMr. B?land.]
through Canada and then departs from our shores cannot receive an impression of monotony as respects our ethnical conditions. Ethnically there is nothing monotonous about Canada. You meet the French and the Scotch and the English and the Irish, as well as those people of all those nationalities whom you have invited to become British citizens. You see a variety of religious creeds. But any one who has travelled through this country and has visited homes in Quebec as well as in Western Canada and Ontario must depart firmly convinced that there is a unity of purpose in this country, that purpose being to make Canada broader and happier than it is today.
I do not object to the Government lending financial assistance to a body which would meet, say, annually in one of the large cities of Canada to discuss generally questions of education as affecting all the provinces. But I cannot share the view that my hon. friend's object can be best served by creating a Federal Bureau of Education^

Mr. Speaker, I have followed the debate so far with a great deal of interest. I join the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) in congratulating the mover of the resolution (Mr. Edwards) in that he has steered his ship this afternoon away from the rocks which have been the cause of so many difficulties from time to time in this House. The purpose of my rising, however, is to support the resolution, because as it is worded I can plainly do so. The resolution affirms that "in the opinion of this House, a Federal Bureau of Education should be established." If the resolution read, "that in the opinion of this House, a bureau to promote learning should be established," I would agree with the member for Beauce that in adopting such a resolution we might be encroaching upon provincial rights. The French language is more fortunate than the English in this connection, because it uses the word "instruction" as applying to that which pertains to imparting of knowledge, and "education" as applying to that which pertains to matters of the heart, of conscience, of duty, of citizenship.. The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), having mixed to some extent the questions of instruction and education, has probably led my hon. friend from Beauce (Mr. Beland) to come to the conclusion that the Federal Bureau which has been proposed might encroach on constitutional

rights. I agree with the hon. gentleman that the province of Quebec is causing a great deal of envy in the other provinces just now, and that it deserves credit for the attitude it has taken in recent times.
I also agree with him broadly that it is a result of education, and not the result of 'imparted knowledge. That it originates in this case from a certain section of the province of Quebec, is all the more to their credit. I know, as a matter of fact, that it has been the habit of the Roman Catholic church to teach its people, not as something they ought to have as learning, but as a part of their education, that not every man can be rich, not every man can be a philosopher, not every man can reach the highest grade of education, and if therefore through this teaching the people of the province of Quebec to-day are not susceptible to the emissaries who have created difficulty in other provinces of Canada and *all the world over, so much to the credit of the men who are responsible for that education. But that proves my case, and the case of the hon. member for Frontenac, that education is what we need, and that education which has been given to one province in that sense is needed in all the other provinces of the Dominion, not only in that one sense, but in many others. The unfortunate thing is that whenever we have a discussion or a conference on education and discuss educational systems and the effects education should have, we aire all more or less affected by a stroke of paralysis and indicate our weariness by the yawning of jaws. If by a system of education assisted by federal money, by a Federal Bureau-(you can place the bureau in any part of the Dominion you like so long as it will achieve the same results)- 'if by such a system you can prevent us having in the future nonconformists, for instance, who say that all should be nonconformists, socialists from saying to other socialists "You shall say there is no God," and people who say that we shall make Liberals out of Liberals and Tories out of Tories as a necessity, then a Federal Bureau of Education will have its use. Ruskin said:
" Education does not mean teaching- the people to know what they do not know; it means teaching them to behave as they do not behave."
, Dr. Johnson says:
Opinions once received are seldom recalled for examination. Having been once supposed to he right, they are never discovered to be erroneous.
This is as true of false opinions as of sound ones. The nation then, if wisely directed, will demand a national system of education whose main purpose is to produce good citizens, -attention to be given, not to what is to be taught so much as to what is to be caught; not to the amount learned by the child, so much as the thought acquired. All of us learn the facts and acquire the skill we need through life itself-Most of us learn by study, and not by teaching, or only by teaching as the result of study. Give a man an opportunity and he will easily learn. The difficulty lies in establishing a desire to study in the individual. It cannot be inculcated as it is infectious-. Create in the nation an emotional belief in education and the desire for education will arise. If our public schools have ideals of good form more than cold ambition for intellectual success, the result will be as it has been in England. "I will do it" promises the South American. "On the word of an Englishman?" inquires his friend. "Yes, on the word of an-Englishman." The public opinion of our public -schools is the medium through which, honest English spirit is most efficiently cultivated. We need as well a larger learning, fuller intellectual life, and a wider diffusion of every sort of skill.
Let -me give an instance of what I really mean by a Bureau of Education. It is taken from the annual report for 1913 of the chief medical officer of the Board of Education in England, page 237, wherein it is related how the children of the Hughes Fields Girls (Council School at Greenwich were taught the rudiments of cleanliness and decent living. The report says:
This school is situated in an extremely poor-part of Deptford. Indeed, the condition of the children attending the school was at one time so trying to those who came in contact with them, that the staff were constantly absent through illness. It became impossible to keep supply teachers more than a few days, and the attendance was freauently as low as 60 to 70 per cent for the whole year. Accordingly, nine years ago a new regime was introduced, con-sitting of lessons in hygiene, inspections, and doing things. The lessons may be imagined They were only given to the older children. The Inspections were daily; boots, clothes, hair, hands, nails, handkerchiefs, the basins and towels with which they washed, all were looked at, and the dirty and untidy were shamed by being put right in the presence of the class This was the real educational force. A new public opinion was created, and it was fostered by such exercises as tooh-brush drill, nailtrimming drill, and so forth. The children' were also asked at what hour they went to bed the previous night, and whether they had slept with an open window. The master of another large school invokes the aid of public opinion in the same direction by having a prepared blackboard

in each class room with spaces for the insertion of figures detailing the number present with clean boots, collars, nails, teeth, handkerchiefs and " open windows last night."
The result of this effort after nine years at the Deptford school is thus described:
The attendance now averages over 92 per cent, the' members of the staff are no longer frequently absent on sick leave, or desirous of obtaining new posts; the children now bear the closest inspection, and are able to progress normally in the ordinary subjects. Taking the school as a whole, the effect of these methods can be best seen by passing from the lowest class to the highest, thus starting with dirty teeth, bitten nails, unkempt hair and untidy clothes, we reach clean teeth, properly tended hands and hair, and neatly mended clothes. The happy air and healthy looks of the children make it hard to believe that this is actually a school of " peculiar difficulty." The children obviously love the school, and from being a place avoided by teachers it has become a field of happy and useful work.
Such are the results brought about by a healthy public opinion.
In many schools the children who systematically attend school with clean boots, clean collars, hair tidily done, teeth brushed, and who sleep with their windows open, are named " specials," and there is a great rivalry amongst them to be so classed.
That is an example of what I deem to be the business of a Federal Bureau of Education which forbids that I should annoy the House with any further illustrations, but as the Educational Conference held at Winnipeg has been referred to, let me point out to the hon. member for Beauee (Mr. Belaud) as well as to others, what that conference really understood by the question of Education.
Addresses were given on the following subjects: The moral and spiritual less ms of the war loi Canadian Education; The School and the Development of Moral Purpose; The Development of a National Character through Education; The Essential Factors in Education; Auxiliaries to the Schools in Moral Training; The Function of the Public School in Character Formation; Education and Reconstruction; The School and Industrial Relationships; The Relation of the School to Democracy; The School and the Newer Citizens of Canada; The Ethics of Christ in the Life of the Nation..
Will it be contended by the hon. member for Beauee (Mr. Belaud) or those who are opposed to the establishment of a Bureau of Education that any of these subjects which were discussed at that conference forms part of the curriculum of education in any province? These are subjects which are not taught except as part of the higher

courses in universities, and to the general public they < an only be imparted by example. The lessons which are to be conveyed by these subjects can reach the average student cr pupil only through the example of those who take the lead. Mr. Speaker, I think that the resolution as drafted is one that should receive the hearty support of this House. I had occasion last session to speak on the amount of money that has been expended by the Federal -Government in regard to matters that come entirely within the purview of the provinces, and if it is advisable for the Dominion Government to supply money for the purpose of assisting agriculture in the provinces there is just as grave reason why the Dominion Government should spend a considerable sum of money for any purpose that tends to the development of such a -national character as should exist in this country. We have a strong and virile people; we have health as -well as wealth. Let ns therefore have a keen, and clear sense of our national purpose.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with close attention to the excellent speeches that have been delivered this afternoon upon this important subject, and with a great deal of interest to the arguments advanced in support of the resolution. Hon. gentlemen are to be congratulated on their efforts. I also listened with much interest to the arguments which were advanced in support of the resolution moved in this House about ten days ago by the hon. member for South Perth (M-r. -Steele). These two resolutions have very much in common, and I desire to 'associate myself with all that has -been said in support of them. Any movement that has for its ohject the improvement of the educational facilities for Canadianizing the foreigner, and improving our system of education throughout the Dominion of Canada, will have my enthusiastic support. No hon. member need 'apologize for supporting the resolution moved and so well presented this afternoon by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). The resolution that, in the opinion of this House, a Federal Bureau of Education should be established at Ottawa, is a very broad one, and one that is comprehensive enough to include every possible phase of the educational problem. It includes the whole field of education in relation to the physical, the intellectual, and the spiritual development of the people. Any system that does not include these three phases of education

[DOT]would not 'be adequate to the needs of the country. The hon. member for Beauce .(Mr. Beland) made some remarks with regard to the spirit of intolerance, and stated that in the province of Quebec there was an absence of.that lamentable national defect. As a resident in Ontario I can honestly say that so far as that province is concerned there is not shortcoming in this respect.
It has been contended that the provinces have exclusive jurisdiction over matters of education within their boundaries. I believe that the provinces, under the terms of the British North America Act, have certain rights with regard to education- rights which it is in no way intended to infringe by the resolution now under discussion. I do not think there is any reason whatever to assume that the intention of the hon. member who has introduced this resolution is tlj,at there shall be any encroachment upon the powers conferred upon the various provinces by the British North America Act. The hon. Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Meighen) said a few days ago that the provinces had certain rights in the matter of education, and in connection with this statement I desire to point out that we have a Federal Department of Public Health, although, according to the terms of the British North America Act, the provinces have jurisdiction in the matter of health. I supported the legislation which established the Federal Health Department because I believed it had a wide field of usefulness; but it does not interfere with the provinces, although it assists them in educating the people in the laws of health. Similar arguments can be advanced in support of this Federal Bureau of Education, which can also work in harmony with the provinces, and assist in co-ordinating a unifying system of education throughout the country. I believe it is essential to the future of Canada that we should have a unified system of education, 'with common text-books in all the public schools, in order that the children might grow up together with common sentiments and ideals, .and a common conception of national duty. This is an educational campaign. It has for its object the stability and progress of the Canadian people. It aims at concentrating the public mind on a national ideal that will unite the people in a common purpose, namely, the making of Canada into one of the greatest and foremost nations of the civilized world. This is an object that should receive the enthusiastic
support of every citizen who is loyal to the traditions of this Dominion.
Ever since the dawn of civilization, statesmen in every land have realized that one of the greatest factors in the stability and progress of any people is the influence exerted by educational institutions. Our universities, colleges, high schools, and more particularly the public schools are every day instilling inti} the minds of children those thoughts, ideals and aspirations which will influence their whole lives and have a powerful effect upon the future character of Canadian citizenship. If the Fathers of Confederation made any mistake in drafting the British North America Act, it was, I think, in relation to our school system. I have no desire, Sir, to be harsh in my criticism of the Fathers of Confederation. I have nothing but respect and honour for their memory, for I conceive them to be amongst the great men this country has produced. It goes without saying that they had the interest of Canada at heart. They did not realize-perhaps they could not realize-that this country of diversified character and climate, of vast distances and varying commercial interests, peopled of necessity by different races and creeds, would need some common bind, some steady unifying influence to cement together the various links in our long national chain. Our greatest need is a silken cord of education stretched across this country from Halifax to Vancouver, vibrating with a uniform national sentiment, permeating the atmosphere of every public school, instilling Canadianism into the minds of those various races and creeds amongst our budding population who, in the next generation will control the destiny of Canada.
There never has been a time in the history of this country when education of a national character was more essential to peace and progress than now. There is a national consciousness awakening in the mind of the people and the time is psychological for the launching of a great educational campaign.
At no time has there ever been a reason given to prove the need of education that does not exist intensified and accentuated to-day.
*Christianity has been spreading the Gospel education for 2,000 years, proclaiming it from thousands of pulpits, by thousands of eloquent divines and still the need exists as never before. This old world is just beginning to rub its eyes, awakening from its slumbers to. a realization of the truth. Awakening to the fact that truth and jus-

tiee, tempered with love, and supported by honour, is the only sure foundation for permanence.
In support of my contention in the cause of education, I would cite no less a personage than that of His Majesty, the King. I have before me a Canadian press despatch of July 31 last which is as follows:
His Ma jesty King George made another notable speech yesterday in replying to congratulations from a joint deputation of the London County Council and Non-conformist ministers at Buckingham Palace.
The King said: " The awakened consciousness of the nation demanded new developments and the removal of many grave defects in our social system. I am confident that our free and representative loyal institutions will be equal to the task.
" Let me recall to you some things that are specially within my thoughts.
" Of housing I have already spoken to representative authorities. I need only repeat my earnest desire that nothing will be left undone to meet the needs of the moment, and to realize those better ideals for the home life of our people which can alone make possible a real improvement in conditions. Great are the needs and great the opportunity. I am convinced also that nothing is more essential to national prosperity and happiness than education. The potentialities, physical, mental and spiritual, of every community should be developed to the fullest extent. A true education would embrace all these; would cultivate them all in due proportion, and would transform our national life in a generation."
I heartily endorse the sentiments expressed by His Majesty and I regard it as a sign that democracy is making progress when the most exalted personage in the world takes this attitude on the question of education. Long may His Majesty live to exert his exalted influence in the interest of the common people of his far-flung Empire.
The great danger of this country, and indeed of the whole world, is selfishness, individual and national. The great war with its ruthless force, its abhorrent brutality, its disregard of human suffering and of individual and national rights, has let loose a flood of evil, selfish passions that threaten to submerge and to annihilate the finer instincts of the human heart. We are still in the gloaming of that awful struggle that deluged the Continent of Europe with the blood of all the races of mankind. Tlie bitter wounds of outraged humanity are not healed and they find expression in the unrest and unjust demands of class and community. Society, the conventions, the moral and spiritual nature of the human race have been changed and we are groping about for a new standard of life. A new social order and a regenerated world are in the making. Never in our history did we
[Ml. .Andei-uon.]
have greater need for a wise guiding force to direct the minds of the people in a proper channel. Time is an element in the cure of all diseases whether of the individual or of the state, and time and wise educational remedies, if properly applied, will bring unity and peace out Of discord and strife.
The fundamental principle that underlies democracy is education. Democracy implies education since it is a government of thfe people by the people. If democracy must be made safe for the people then the people must be educated to be safe for themselves. Free peoples of the earth must be educated to understand the duties of good citizenship and the principles of responsible government, if democracy is to fulfil its mission and civilization stand the test of material progress. The group system of government towards which we are drifting is not democratic. The group system, as we have it in the province of Ontario, representative of a minority, is essentially autocratic. In this connection I would quote Bishop Bidwell, who in addressing the Anglican Synod in the city of Kingston, said:
Group System Not Democracy.
" The group selfishness, masking itself under so-called democratic forms of government, is little better than despotism. True democracy does not mean that the majority shall relentlessly impose its will upon the minority. It is the government of the people by their duly accredited representatives in the interests of the whole people, in which the rights of minorities and individuals are duly protected and observed. In the support of government of this kind the Christian spirit is of the utmost importance."
I might add to the statement of Bishop Bidwell that neither does democracy mean that the minority shall relentlessly impose its will on the majority. Minority rule is autocratic rule which controlled Ejirope for centuries. "A spirit of liberty"-said Chan-ning,-"is not as multitudes imagine a jealousy for our particular rights but a respect for the rights of others and an unwillingness that any one, whether high or low, should be,trampled under foot." This, Mr. 'Speaker, surely is or should be the spirit of democracy, but it is not the spirit of all those who shout in.the name of democracy. We have had ample evidence ' during the last five years to prove that those who shout loudest in the name of d mocraey are themselves autocrats at heart. Democracy to them is a license to do as they please, regardless of the rights and privileges of other. That was exemplified in the Winnipeg strike of last year. An

autocracy in the name of democracy usurped the will of the people. A minority, the minions of a class, ruled the city regardless of the rights and privileges of its citizens. The city was coerced into submission and civic and provincial government was defied. There was no rioting because the citizens submitted quietly to the abrogation of their rights and sought a refhedy by constitutional means. Such a condition was intolerable and could not long be endured, and both factions to the dispute are to he congratulated on the wise councils that prevailed. The ending of the Winnipeg strike is an eloquent tribute to the sanity and moderation of the Canadian people. Now that the parties concerned have been given a fair trial, found guilty and sentenced, I trust that the Department of Justice of the Dominion Government will not interfere with the sentence of the court.
Constitutional means, however, do not always prevail. Russia to-day is an example of democracy gone mad. It is a case of majority rule with vengeance as its motto. Democracy is so attenuated that each individual is an autocrat to the limit of his own physical powers. Pre-historie man has been resurrected and is running naked and vile in the heart of a 20th century civilization. Bolshevism is a leach that seeks its sustenance from the labour of others and breaks down all institutions of justice and order to fill its sordid stomach on the spoils of thrift. M. Erlich, a Frenchman and a Socialist, who was stationed at Petrograd as a member of the French Mission from August T7 to April '19 has this to say of Bolshevism:
I am and remain Socialist, and that is why I withdraw from a party which does not justify the title it bears, and which is sinking more and more into a Bolshevism, which is the savage negation of the Socialist ideal.
Mr. Erlich, a Socialist, has left his party on account of its sympathy with the ideal of Bolshevism. He may some day realize that socialism itself is a weed that thrives in the garden of indolence. Socialism would destroy initiative, and reduce all to the same level by depriving energy of the fruits of its labours. Such a system would put a penalty on thrift, and a premium on laziness. Socialism would arrive at its ideals by a system of paternal government which in a generation or two would produce a race of weaklings. As the people are, so is the nation. If the individuals of a race are weaklings amongst individuals, then the nation will be a weakling among nations. I would take this opportunity of warning the Government to resist the agitation for
paternal legislation. Such legislation will destroy initiative, individual independence, and self reliance which characteristics are a people's greatest asset in the pursuit of national greatness.
I am not in favour, Mr. Speaker, of too many restrictions being placed on individual liberty. You cannot make a people good by law; they cannot be made righteous by branding their follies as crimes. Legislation in advance of education and public sentiment is dangerous and defeats its own end. Neither am I in favour of legislation which tends to make certain classes wards of the state, which deprives them of the necessity of providing a living for themselves-it destroys .their independence and self-respect. Our laws, Mr. Speaker, should aim at producing men and women of independent minds who can stand erect and alone, working out their own emancipation from penury and want, by giving them equality of opportunity to develop the talents with which they have been endowed.
This leads us to the question of the alien population which is within our country, and forms a very important part of the people of the Dominion. In 1911, from the figures that I placed on Hansard last year, there were 752,732 alien people in this Dominion. Of these 303,680 came from the United States, and 370,389 from continental Europe. From 1912 to 1918, 603,468 foreign-born came into Canada front the United States, and.384,967 from continental Europe, so that at the end of 1918 we had in the Dominion 1,662,497 people who were born outside of the Dominion, that is, not British subjects. The most important problem for this country at the present time is the education an4 assimilation into the social and economic life of the alien people who have come here to live. This is a vital question which it is absolutely essential that the Dominion Government should grapple with and solve. In this connection, the Federal Bureau of Education would be of the utmost importance and could give material assistance to the Government in the solution of this very difficult problem.
We can learn much from the lessons of the Great War in relation to thid question. That great conflagration has cast a lurid glare on the deplorable conditions which existed and still exist in Europe. European radicalism makes it absolutely essential that we shall be more critical of the class of immigrants we admit to citizenship. We cannot any longer regard the immigrant simply from the economic point of view. We must take

cognizance of his political character and reputation.
Let us take a short glimpse of Europe as it is to-day after four and a half years of war and one and a half years of peace, speaking advisedly of the peace. There is a good deal of ebulition still in these disturbed countries. The tornado has passed and the international storm has subsided, but the waves'of discontent are still running high. There are signs, however, that the calm which should follow the storm may come in another year or two.
Illiteracy will mean inability to read and write in any language. You will admit, Mr. Speaker, that this is a very low standard. In most of* the countries the age taken is ten years and over, although in one or two, the age limit is lower than ten. years. In Canada, for instance, we are rated as having 11.45 per cent of illiteracy over five years of age. Even in the West educated countries children between five and 10 years cannot be said to be able to read and write. I draw the attention of the Government to this rating in the hope it may be corrected. Inability to read and write in any language indicates that a person is unable to understand the written word and has no means of communication with his fellowman except by word of mouth.
The study of illiteracy the world over has some interesting features. It shows that people of northern climates are better edu- [DOT] cated than those of southern climates. People in warm countries have a higher percentage of illiteracy than those in the cold countries; that the dark races are more illiterate than the white; that brunettes are more illiterate than blondes and that women are more illiterate than men. These world-wide conditions are reflected in the conditions of a country. Take the United, States for instance which has a great variety of climate. We find there that the people living in the States having a warm climate are more illiterate than those in the colder states. It also shows that this applies to the white population as well as to the dark population; it also shows that the-women of the United States are more illiterate than the men, although the percentage of difference is less than in other countries. In America the sexes are more nearly on an equality in regard to illiteracy than in Europe.
In the continent of Europe, illiteracy is as follows:
Russia 69 per cent over ten years and 61.7 per cent of army are illiterate. Bixty-
two adult people out of every hundred are unable to understand the written word. They have no means of getting knowledge on any subject even on every day affairs, except by word of mouth. Stories oft repeated get wide of the truth. We ip this country depend upon our press and yet the press either wilfully or unintentionally does not always print what is correct.
Russia has the highest percentage of illiteracy amongst its adult population of any country in Europe. This is significant in view of the chaotic conditions of her internal affairs as the result of the war.
Take the Balkan states, that hot-bed of European wars, and we find that Turkey has no statistics, presumably because the country has not enough interest in education to compile statistics. The statistics for the other Balkan states are:
Roumania, 60.6 per cent over 10 years; 41 per cent of army illiterate.
Bulgaria, 65.5 per cent over 10 years; 25.4 per cent of army.
Greece, 57.2 per cent over 10 years; 30 per cent of army.
Serbia, 78-9 per cent over 7 years; 43-4 per cent of army.
Albania and Montenegro-No statistics.
These figures are illuminating. The Balkan states are continually embroiling Europe in their quarrels. The dense ignorance of the people renders them an easy mark for agitators and disturbers of the peace.
The Near Balkans.
Hungary, 33 per cent over 6 years; Illiterate.
Italy, 37 per cent over 10 years; 31 per cent of army.
Austria, 18 per cent over 11 years.
These percentages indicate high rate of illiteracy. There will be many people in these countries having no proficiency in education though not classed as illiterate. These people are a menace to the peace of Europe, and the League of Nations will have no success until they are educated to understand the principles of responsible government. They are not fit for democracy ; they are not ready to govern themselves. It is questionable if they will be good material to transplant into Canada. Are they desirable immigrants for this country?
Germany, .05 per cent of the army Illiterate.	.
Prussia, .02 per cent of the army illiterate.
Germany is in a class by herself; her people the victims of Kultur, were educated

for a particular purpose. From the cradle they were taught to have one ideal, and that ideal was not lost sight of in all branches of their educational system. With such a people in central Europe, educated for war, surrounded, by illiterate peoples, conflict was inevitable. The only marvel is that it was delayed so long. Germany, although in the midst of revolution which has swept her centuries old autocratic system of government from office, has accomplished it almost without bloodshed. This is a remarkable achievement, never before equalled in the history of the world.
It is an indication of the restraining influences of education upon the minds of the people in times otf great stress. .
Take the neutral nations of Europe, those in the immediate vicinity of the maelstrom of war, those nations that were not bound by entangling alliances compelling them to take part in the conflict and that were able to resist all influences to drag them into it.
Switzerland, .03 per cent of army illiterate.
Denmark, .02 per cent of army illiterate.
Sweden, .02 per cent of army illiterate.
The Netherlands, .08 per cent of army illiterate.
A remarkably high percentage of education exists in all these countries; they have the lowest percentages of illiteracy in the world. Almost all the people are able to understand the written word, and are thus capable of being informed on public affairs and restrained from excesses in times of stress.
From these figures and the conditions of social unrest and revolution in Enrope it is easy to draw conclhsions. The handwriting is plain on the wall. The uneducated peoples are running riot and perpetrating untold atrocities on each other. Life and property and t/he sanctity of the home have no protection. Woman is a slave; the subject of barter between sensual brutes. The animal propensities of the human race have gained ascendency over the intellectual and spiritual.
The League of Nations will have a large field for usefulness in assisting to have these people educated in the duties of good citizenship and the principles of responsible government. In fact a League of Nations might have a large field of usefulness in teaching the members of the American Congress the duties and necessities of peace. Those members have not been sufficiently impressed by the great tragedies of the war to be raised above the amenities of political strife. They are apparently more interested in discrediting their President than
they are in the necessity of bringing peace to a blood-spattered world.
Educationists in this country should view with alarm any large influx of peoples from amongst the illiterates of Europe. These illiterates should be scrutinized with the greatest care when coming into this country. It will be a difficult matter to keep out all undesirables; those, however who have grave physical and mental defects can be easily detected. The illiterate will present no difficulty, but some of those illiterates may be desirable citizens. Illiteracy is not synonymous with immorality and depravity. A stolid hard working man of moderate views and good common sense is much to be preferred to the smart propagandist.
This is where common sense and a natural human instinct will be invaluable in an immigration officer and will be a great service to this country. The educated agitators are the most dangerous, and they should be followed into their homes and, if engaged in spreading questionable doctrines, should be promptly deported. I have no sympathy with officials who treat these agitators leniently. They do not understand leniency and mistake it for timidity and fear of their class. Given a fair trial and proven guilty, they should be hustled out of the country without ceremony.
Not only do we need greater care in admitting the immigrant, but we must look after him better when he settles here. Let any honourable member of this House imagine himself an immigrant in a new country amongst an alien people unac* quainted with the language, depending upon his own labour for existence, ignorant of the customs and habits and laws of the country; open to deception, to fraud, and to ill treatment by designing persons and tell me if he would not follow any of his own people, even if he were an agitator. We cannot blame these people too much in their ignorance for paying heed to agitators in their own class. The remedy is, get rid of the agitator. Most of. these people are anxious to become good citizens if they knew how. They will, of course, have memories of their own lands and such is but natural; the longing of their hearts for friends and scenes of their youth cannot be stilled by law. You cannot change the current of the soul by Act of Parliament, they must be led to a higher plane of life by education. It is, therefore, important for our people to get alive to the problem of the new comer and organize for his protection and education and assimilation into

the life of the country; start from the day he lands to Canadianize him and follow him wherever he goes. Every community should have its committee to look after the alien. With regard to this alien question I would like to read a short passage, Mr. Speaker, from an article that appeared in a western paper, as follows:
There is a deep-seated conviction in the West that any man or woman who is dissatisfied with Canada as to he eternally comparing; it with their " fatherland " and preaching- sedition and intrigue, ought to be, and shall be, sent back to their dear fatherland, at their own expense if they have the money, and at the country's expense if they are broke. There has been ah impression among a good many pretty well-informed people in the West that deportation orders of this alien agitating class have not been as energetically conducted as they might have been, considering the dangerous element that centres around this element west of the lakes
In connection with the assimilation of these people, Mr. Speaker, I desire to quote from an article by Arthur Hamilton relative to conditions in the United States. He writes:
Of all the nationalities represented among the Immigrants in the United States the Germans are by far the hardest to make American.
Ludwig Fulda says in his " American Impressions;" "For children of German parents to speak German is to remain German."
Charles F. Amidon, one of the judges in the Western States, in sentencing a German agitator convicted of sedition, addressed his as follows:
I find that you received your final papers in 1898.	By the oath which you then took
you renounced and abjured all allegiance to Germany and to the Emperor of Germany, and swore that you would bear true faith and allegiance to the United States. Have you done that? No, you have not. You have, instead, cherished everything German, read German, prayed German, sung German. Every thought of your mind and every motion of your heart through all these years has been German. There have been a good many Germans before me in the last month; they have lived in this country like yourself, for ten, twenty, thirty, forty years, and they had to give their- evidence through an interpreter, because they could not speak English.
I want you to understand that when you take the oath of allegiance it means that you begin to sing American songs, read American history and open your life to American- influence. Instead of doing that, you have cherished German ideals and tried to make them everlasting."
This was the opinion of the judge in addressing this German citizen. The question is, shall we give these people who come into our country the franchise? Of course, they will get the privileges of the 
franchise in time, but I think that they should not receive the franchise until they have been given a good education, can speak and write the English language and have been taught to understand and appreciate the principles of democratic government. These people, coming as they do from European countries which have autocratic forms of government, cannot understand democracy, and we must make them understand it. There was a good deal in the remark made by the member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) during the course of his address on the resolution introduced by the member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) to the effect that the franchise should be conferred gradually on these people. First they should be given the municipal franchise; then when they come to be familiar with that, they can be given the provincial franchise, and finally the federal franchise. That would be a good way to enable them to understand the duties of citizenship and the responsibilities of the elector.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I may he pardoned if I wander from the subject under debate for a few moments to extend my congratulations to the architect, the contractor and workmen employed for the wisdom, skill and energy displayed in erecting this magnificent building." As a building of its kind, for the purpose intended, perfect in proportion, stately in design, solid in structure, , elegant in workmanship, complete in detail and unsurpassed in dignified grandeur, it will stand for centuries as a monument to the skill of the workmen and the sagacity and vision of the Canadian people.
This assembly room, generous in proportions and beautiful in adornment, will serve as an inspiration to future generations of Parliamentarians to put forth the best that is in them. Tt will inspire members of Parliament to greater oratorical effort and higher statesmanship. A member rising to address you, Mr. Speaker, in this Chamber, will have instinctively impressed upon him the great responsibility and dignity of the office which he holds. He will realize that in speaking here he is addressing not the members of Parliament and the citizens in the gallery, but great Canadian people. It will help him to realize that he represents more than the citizens of the small constituency who are responsible for his presence in this House. It will help him to realize that he is a representative Canadian, a citizen of a great country just beginning to extend its influence beyond its shores into the sisterhood of nations.

If I might venture a criticism of this Chamber, I would voice my disappointment in its acoustic properties. I am fearful that my voice cannot penetrate with distinctness into the farthermost reaches of this spacious hall. There are so many nooks and corners, so many projections and cavities, so much space to fill,' that it seems impossible for one small voice adequately to fill the void without those artificial aids of arched domes and round corners to intensify sound.
Taken as a whole, this stately edifice, the product of the brain and handicraft of man, is a work of art, vying for supremacy over the beautiful in nature which has been so lavishly bestow-ed on this picturesque section of the Dominion of Canada.
The building itself is a liberal education in Canadian history, and will serve to keep alive and to perpetuate those traditions of life and character which are the foundation of a nation's greatness.
Members on both sides of this House have expressed themselves on the question of Canadian unity and deplored' its absence between the two predominating races in this country. Unity is absolutely essential to the future progress of the Canadian people, and this building will lend itself admirably as a factor in- that unity. Parliament is the greatest educational influence we have for the building up of a sound, sane, progressive citizenship. The people of this country look to the members of Parliament for leadership on all lines connected with the national welfare. They are expected to be alive to our possibilities, conscious of the potentialities of the national domain, interested in human progress and ready to defend and to maintain those institutions of Government that are the people's guarantee of national life, liberty and progress. The. foundation of a nation's greatness is the mentality of its people. A sane mind in a sound body, morally clean and spiritually pure, is the highest type of human being.
Take such a people as I have described, place them on the northern half of the American continent, under the influence of its climate, surrounded by its wealth of forest, field and mine; educate them in the arts, the science and the duties of citizenship, and in less than a century you will have a people that will extend their influence to the four corners of the earth, and that influence will be for the general benefit of mankind. We have here a country which is unsurpassed in natural wealth, waiting only the brain and the hand to
unlock its stores. It is the duty of the Canadian people to prove themselves worthy of their great heritage. It is the duty of this Parliament to prove it has the wisdom, the vision and the initiative to point the way that will start Canada on the road to her high destiny.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks on the resolution which is before the House will be very brief indeed. It is not my intention to dwell upon the necessity of education in any country, nor do I intend to speak on the merits or demerits of the educational facilities in the various provinces of this country. The ht>n. gentleman (Mr. Anderson) who preceded me, spoke eloquently of the needs of greater education in the world, referring especially to the conditions created by the various new doctrines such as Bolshevism, and so forth, and I agree with what he said in that respect. At no time in the history of the world has a sound education been more needed than at present. He even suggested that the League of Nations should look after the education of the peoples of the world. That only shows how hard it is, once we start infringing upon the constitution, to know where to stop. The mover of the resolution (Mr. Edwards) wants the Federal Parliament to , have a say in educational matters. His seconder (Mr. Anderson) wants the,League of Nations to have a say in these matters. For myself I would just as soon have the League of Nations control education in this country as have the Federal Parliament control it, because the Treaties of Peace have shown that the protection of national minorities is well looked after by the various statesmen of the world-better than it has been in many instances in this country. However, it is not my purpose to dwell on that phase of the question.
The British North America Act was an agreement between various British colonies which on certain questions had diverse interests, diverse views, diverse feelings and diverse opinions. Indeed, these diversities were so great that it was thought at one time they would constitute an insuperable obstacle to the final consummation of Confederation. No question perhaps was more mooted than that of education, and it is

quite natural that it should be so, because on the question of education are always dependent all matters relating to race, language and religion. Men there were in my own province belonging both to the Catholic majority and to the English-speaking Protestant minority who viewed with fear and alarm the provisions of the British North America Act, and it is a matter of history that the provisions of the educational clauses of that Act guaranteeing the protection of minorities as to denominational schools were placed in the Act at, the special request of the English-speaking minority of the province of Quebec. At all events, the matter of education was left to the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces, subject to a certain limitation. Section 93 of the British North America Act reads in part as follows:
In and for each province the Legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to education, subject and according to the following provisions :-
1. Nothing in any such lavs' shall prejudicially affect any right or privilege with respect to denominational schools which any class of persons have by law in the province at the Union.
Subsections 2, 3 and 4 give the remedy for a minority which might be pressed in the enjoyment of their privileges. With that understanding Confederation was agreed to. The British North America Act was an agreement between various British colonies by virtue of which those colonies agreed to surrender to a central power-the Federal Parliament-some of their powers and rights, and those colonies reserved to themselves certain other powers and rights which are specifically enumerated in the British North America Act. Education ,is one of those matters which were specifically and emphatically reserved. I am sure that no hon. gentleman in this House will challenge my statement when I say that without this reservation with regard to education, Confederation would never have been achieved. ^
I also make the statement, and submit the proposition, that the provinces within the limit of their jurisdiction are as supreme in their authority as this Parliament within the sphere of its jurisdiction, as supreme even as the Imperial Parliament. Within the limit of their jurisdiction they have absolute home rule, and they will continue to have it, notwithstanding any hon. gentlemen's efforts to the contrary.

I did not quite catch what the hon. gentleman said. Was he referring to me in his remark "notwithstand-

ing any hon. gentleman's efforts to the contrary?"

No, I was speaking in a general way. I desire to quote the words of Mr. Justice Riddell, who is certainly a constitutional authority, to be found at page 99 of his volume "The Constitution of Canada." He is quoting words used by himself in the case of Smith vs. city of London:
The powers of the legislature of the province are the same in intension, though not in extension, as those of the Imperial Parliament. The legislature as limited in the territory in which it may legislate and in the subjects; the Imperial Parliament is not-that is the whole difference. .	.	. The power and jurisdiction of
Parliament is so transcendent and absolute that it cannot be confined either for causes or persons within any bounds.
I could quote the opinion of many other judges, but I shall content myseif with giving the words of Lord Carnarvon in 1875. This House had sent an address to Her Majesty the Queen asking he. to make certain representations to. the Legislature of New Brunswick with regard to certain educational difficulties in that province, and here is the answer made by Lord Carnarvon, who was then British Secretary of State for the 'Colonies. The words will be found in Todd's "Parliamentary Government in the British Colonies," page 462:
He could only express a strong hope that the ruling majority in New Brunswick might be disposed so to exercise their undoubted rights as to remove all reasonable causes of complaint, and so avoid the " serious inconvenience of bringing under public discussion in the Dominion Legislature a controverted question which may possibly engender much heat and irritation, and over which it has no jurisdiction."
What is the only* conclusion that must be drawn? It is that the Federal Parliament has no authority in educations! matters other than those conferred upon it by section 93 of the British North America Act.	The powers of such a Federal
Bureau of Education as proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards), to remain ' within the jurisdiction of this Parliament would be confined to dealing with the legislatures of the various provinces respecting the rights and privileges of the religious minorities with regard to denominational schools. Surely that is not the aim and intention of my hon. friend. It is certainly not that which he seeks to remedy.
I would ask my hon. friend from Fron-tenac why he comes back here every session with a resolution which he knows cannot be accepted by this House? Last year his resolution was in favour of the

establishment of a national system of nonsectarian schools. That resolution could not be adopted without leading to the disruption of Confederation. His resolution this year does not go quite so far; it is not a direct but a flank attack, but it is just as much against the jurisdiction of this Parliament and against the constitution of Canada as was his resolution last year. What purpose is my hon. friend wishing to serve? A few weeks ago, in connection with a resolution on the Order Paper asking for an amendment to the British North America Act to give this Parliament extra-territorial jurisdiction for its laws, it was suggested in this House that we should ask an amendment to the constitution of Canada to enable this Parliament to amend its own constitution with the unanimous consent of the provinces. I think that principle is a sound one. This great country cannot forever be crossing the sea for the purpose of begging small, petty amendments to the constitution, with reference, for instance, to the superannuation of a judge, or other matters of like importance. Our constitutional level must be as high as that of South Africa or Australia. I repeat, I think the principle is sound. But various authorities objected to the proposal among them being the Attorney General of Quebec, in a telegram which was published in the newspapers. Why should it be so? Simply because there are men in this country who seem to be anxious to regard treaties, agreements and pledges as mere " scraps of paper," and because those who have something to protect are determined that they will not relinquish that protection which is conceded them by the Imperial Parliament. I repeat that I would personally be in favour of any suggestion to give to this country the right to amend its own constitution. But proposals such as that which my hon. friend from Fiontenac (Mr. Edwards) puts forward would block the way of Canada in any request which she might make for greater autonomy, and would only serve to strengthen in many people the resolve not to part with the guarantee which they have through the Imperial Parliament. The hon. gentleman states that this Federal Bureau would not encroach upon the rights of the provinces. Well, Sir, in my opinion, which I think is a sound one, the mere establishment of such a bureau would constitute an undoubted infringement of the rights of the provinces. It would be exactly the same as if the Imperial Parliament should try to establish a bureau to control our trade &nd our immigration laws under the pretense that it did not infringe our rights in these matters. Would any Canadian tolerate such an act as that? We would not; and i say that the provinces will not stand for any supervision such as that proposed by my hon. friend.	-

Does my hon. friend
state that this resolution proposes a supervision or control in regard to matters of education?

I do not- see what other object it can have. The bureau would have some work to do, it would have some purpose to achieve and it could hot achieve that purpose without exercising control or supervision over the work of the provinces. My hon. friend stated as a precedent the fact that this Parliament granted money towards the improvement of the roads, towards the development of agriculture, and for purposes of that kind. Well, I am not surprised at that. If hon. members will look up Hansard they will see that when these matters were under discussion in the House I for one predicted that some one later on would contend that the legislation then going through the House would establish a precedent that would enable this Parliament to interfere with the rights of the provinces in the matter of education. It was wrong for Parliament to interfere with those matters, but hon. members opposite at that time were emphatic in the assertion that they had nothing to do with education and that our fears in that respect were without any foundation. Events, however, have shown who were right. The hon. member gave us the United States as an example in the matter of education, and informed us that there was in that country a Federal Bureau of Education that achieved remarkable success. Of course, our situation is by no means identical with that of the United States; there is a certain difference between the conditions as they are in the two countries. But speaking only from the point of view of results, does my hon. friend not know that the fact was established that 34 per cent of the American soldiers who enlisted could neither read nor write? Is that the " great success " which he says has been achieved by the National Bureau of Education in the United States? I think that Canada's record in this respect is much higher than that of our neighbours to the south of us. One more remark, Mr. Speaker, and I shall conclude. My-hon. friend spoke of the desirability

of national unity. In this wish I heartily join.
Before the hon. member proceeds, may I enquire of him as to the source of his authority for the statement that 34 per cent of the American soldiers were illiterate?

I read the statement
in the American newspapers at the time of its publication.
And it was not denied.

I say, Mr. Speaker,
that I am in complete sympathy with the statement that it is desirable for us to attain national unity. But the only way in which we can secure that unity is by respecting the rights, feelings and privileges of our fellow citizens in this country. There are questions upon which we are bound to disagree. It has been the decree of Providence that this country should be inhabited by people of various races and creeds. We cannot avoid that condition of things. We must face and accept it, and we must accept it in a spirit of tolerance, charity and good-will. Let my hon. friend and myself let all good citizens in this country, agree to disagree on these questions. It is not necessary that we should have identical opinions on all questions; it is impossible for us to agree on some of them. I do not hope, nor have I the presumption to believe, that it is possible to convince my hon. friend that he is wrong in his way of thinking and that I am right, and I give him my word of honour that he will not convince me that he is right in the opinions he has expressed.
I will not try.

Let us both agree to
disagree on that point, and we may be good Canadians, both of us, as our children will be, notwithstanding that they may differ on some questions. Mr. Speaker, let us build in this country an adamantine wall against prejudice and intolerance. Let us respect one another's opinions and convictions, and in the name of common sense, at this particular period of our history, let this Federal Parliament confine its attention to those matters that are peculiarly within its province; for I believe that it has enough affairs of its own, affairs within the limits of its own jurisdiction, without going outside those limits and endeavouring to do the work of the provinces.

We have men in Saskatchewan, I believe, who would come here and perhaps give some pointers to our friends in Ontario and Quebec, and I have no doubt that our friends in Ontario and Quebec would give some pointers in return. If this bureau did nothing else but bring these men together occasionally and have a systematic discussion of these subjects, I believe, it would do good. I see the advantages and I fail to see the disadvantages. I fail to see that there is any absolute danger. Therefore, I think there would be no harm in trying it and possibly there would be much good. Of course, the question comes up as to whether or not the Government are disposed to vote the necessary sum of money for the purpose. There is one other observation that 1 will have to make in a little while with regard to some of the things which might be done by such a body. The term "bureau" is a very elastic one. It does not necessarily mean a body which will have control over education. The Weather Bureau does not pretend to have any control over the weather, but it is a quite useful institution; and in the same way, I believe, a Buieau of Education might be a useful institution although it might not attempt to control education in the different provinces.
I would not have risen but for one fact. The question comes up here frequently of 89
Canadianizing the so-called foreigner. 1 am not very much in love with the term "foreigner" but still I shall use it for want of a better term. I believe that is one thing that such a bureau might possibly deal with. Just what would be done I am not prepared to say, but at least we would have through that bureau a way of getting together men from the different provinces and men of different nationalities or extractions. I have had letters from a Presbyterian clergyman in my constituency who is a pure-bred Hungarian and who ministers to the Hungarian congregation on that line. That man is tremendously anxious that something should be done. He sees the need amongst his own people. He fears that if we do not get together and make a united effort to better conditions they are going to be worse instead of better. I know a great many thoroughly well-educated, up-to-date men, of European nationality-enemy nationality, if you like, -in my constituency. They are well-read, well-posted men who could give us some assistance.
I am afraid that we approach this subject with the idea that all the wisdom is centred within ourselves and that these men have none of it, that we have to teach them. If we would approach them with the idea not only that we can teach them something but that they can teach us something we might get somewhere. The sooner we give up the idea that we know it all and that these men know nothing the sooner we will be in a position to do something in the direction of making these people good citizens of the country. We have been told that the foreigner would respond to our appeal. The foreigner will respond to our appeal, and very readily, if we make that appeal in the proper spirit. If we are going to make it in that spirit of hate that we see manifested in this House sometimes, we are not going to gain much. We had better get clear of that feeling right now. If we are going to teach these people true Canadianism we must make a beginning by showing them that we have the spirit of true Canadianism within ourselves.' If we have not the spirit of democracy and of brotherhood, which should be the basis of Canadian nationality, amongst ourselves, the farther away we keep from these people the better. We must have the proper spirit within ourselves. Then, we are in a position to teach them something.
A great many people have told us at different times in this House that they have



been teachers. The hon. gentleman who introduced this motion (M?. Edwards) to-ld us that he bad been a teacher. There are quite a number of gentlemen in this House who have been teachers, and I am satisfied that if a census were taken it would be found that a majority of the members had at some time been either teachers of public schools or trustees of school hoards. Let us take the trustees. I have had some experience. I know that when we undertook to engage teachers we wanted to find out what these teachers knew; we wanted t-o have reports from people who knew not only what their educational qualifications were but what sort of people they were- their characters. One of the first things that it was necessary to find out was Whether the applicant for appointment as a teacher was a lover of children. The school board took the ground that unless the teacher had a fondness for children, it did not want to know anything about him. I think a school board is very foolish to engage a teacher Who has not a fondness for children. Applying this principle to the question now under discussion I would say that unless we have some love ot fondness for the people whom we undertake to teach we will never teach them anything of importance. We must get into sympathy with those people, with their feelings, their aspirations, their difficulties and their hopes, before we can hope to teach them anything worth while.
These are the few suggestions I wanted to make and I do not think I have anything further to say. I want to emphasize, however, that I see no reason at all why we should fear the formation of such a bureau, for the very good reason that the bureau would not have any power to do the things which we appear to fear it would do.

The resolution calls for the creation ol a National Bureau of Education, and to my mind such a body, unless it were to become absolutely useless, would exercise some form of control over all the provinces. iSpeaking as the representative of a constituency of the province of Quebec, I say we do not desire it, that we do not need it. Our own education system is efficient;
, it is satisfactory to us, and should we need to change or improve it we have within our own province the machinery necessary for that purpose. A backward glance will show that after centuries of experience we have evolved a system which, though not incapable of improvement, compares favourably with that of any other at present existing.
History tells us that when the foundations of permanent settlement were laid, the authorities at Quebec, with the approval and assistance of the French Government, endeavoured by every possible means to promote civilization of the Indians and the intellectual development of the inhabitants. The first boys' school was founded at Quebec .by the Jesuits in 1635; and it should be a matter of pride to all Canadians that a year later-fully a year before the legislature of Massachusetts had decided upon the establishment of Harvard, . -there was in the city of Quebec a classical college. In 1642 the Ursulines founded a girls' boarding school in Quebec. In 1657 we read that the heroic Marguerite Bour-geoys had a school for boys and girls in Montreal. In 1666, we learn, the Montreal Sulpician school was started by the voluntary contributions of the inhabitants. In 1681 there was in full swing at Sillery, a short distance from the city of Quebec, a school devoted to the instruction of the Indians. In the early days of the eighteenth century, schools subsidized by church and state, and aided by enlightened benefactors and testators, spread over the settled parts of the province with great rapidity. All this was put an end to by the conquest when, under the English regime, the religious orders who had hitherto supplied the greatest number of teachers were forbidden to receive members from abroad and

to recruit novices from within the confines of the colony. The property of these reverend gentlemen was, in many cases alienated and the schools closed. Primary and -secondary education was completely disorganized and the ancient inhabitants of the country, aware of the disastrous results of such a system, in 1763 sent in a long series of petitions in which they prayed for public instruction, to which, in their own words, they "hold faster than life itself." -An attempt was made early to control education under a body known as the Royal Institute for the Advancement of Learning. Its real purport, hidden under a pretense of good-will, was to take away the right of teaching from the Canadians, and to establish an educational monopoly, guaranteed by the executive of the English church and paid for by the French-Catholic population, for the upkeep of Protestant and neutral schools. This met with very little success since the native population preferred to keep their children unlettered rather than to trust them to the tender mercies of teachers alien in tongue and in religion. In 1824 the legislature carried the law of Fabrique schools, by which the Fabriques were authorized to devote certain portions of their income to the foundation of a school in each parish. This was more or less satisfactory till in 1859, an -Educational Council, composed of eleven Catholics and four Protestants, was established. In 1875 the constitution of this body was modified by dividing it into two separate and independent religious committees, thus giving to the minority complete control over their own schools. This is the basis of our present system which we are proud to say is highly satisfactory. To quote the words of Dr. Parmalee of the Protestant Council of Instruction :
From this clear recognition oj the necessity, in the interests both of harmony and efficiency, to give the right of separate action, the freedom of control has gradually extended until the Protestant population finds itself in an enviable position in this regard.
Although the British North America Act guaranteed the minority only what it had in 1867, yet its rights and privileges have grown more since that date than previously. An appeal to the sense of justice and fair-play of the majority has produced results which merit praise.
If the minority have no reason for complaint what possible excuse can outsiders have for interference? As for the religious majority, not only are -they satisfied, but any change would be met with the most 89i	j | [DOT] jj
strenuous opposition. For, rightly or wrongly, we firmly believe that religion is the basis o-f all true education, that without religion there can be no morality, and. that all the learning in the world will not produce a good citizen unless he feels himself bound by the sanction of the law ot God as well as that of man. "If you haven't developed a conscience your learning has been in vain; you have furnished arms and armour for that which is evil."
To this theory we adhere most tenaciously. This doctrine we are ready to uphold with all our energy and strength, and we will not-we cannot-alter in any degree an opinion so -well considered and so deeply implanted in our hearts. Shall we be -forced, as are our co-religionists in the United States, to yearly spend millions of dollars over and above the amounts contributed to the state school in order that our children shall receive that instruction which we firmly believe to be an essential preparation to the attainment of -the ideals of good citizenship? Besides, the experience of other nations teaches us that Godless education invariably fails to produce the best results. The lesson of Imperial Rome should not be forgotten. Civilized and cultured as -she was, when atheism became the rage the -finer virtues of the race disappeared and the land of hardy warriors and upright statesmen -became the plaything of the licentious potentate and the debauched tyrant.

In the United States patriotism taught in the schools to the exclusion of religion has become an empty uninspired thing- almost a mere matter of flag-waving and fourth of July fireworks. The politicians control the schools, vote-getting has become more important than morality, material success in this life more to be desired than spiritual happiness in the next. Time does not permit me to quote opinions and statistics showing the failure of the public schools to produce in that country that which at this time it is in most need of-honest, upright, God-fearing citizens, but I have here an article by Harold Bolce published in the Cosmopolitan magazine in 1919, entitled "Blasting at the Rock of Ages." I do not wish to quote the article itself, but the editor's note, which is fully borne out by the facts cited, says:
This is the first of a series of three articles by .Mr. Bolce, who has now completed a study of American colleges extending over two years. What Mr. Bolce sets down here is of the most astounding character. Out of the curricula of American colleges a dynamic movement is upheaving ancient foundations and promising a way for revolutionary thought and life. Those who are not in close touch with the great colleges of the country will be astonished to learn the creeds being fostered by the faculties of our great universities. In hundreds of classrooms it is being taught daily that the decalogue is no more sacred than a syllabus; that the home as an institution is doomed; that there are no absolute evils; that immorality ' is simply an act in contravention of society's accepted standards; that democracy is a failure and the Declaration of Independence only spectacular rhetoric; that the change from one religion to another is like getting a new hat; that moral precepts are passing shibboleths; that conception of right and wrong are as unstable as styles of dress; that wide stairways are open between social levels, but that to the climber children are incumbrances; that the sole effect of prolificacy is to fill tiny graves; and that there can be and are holier alliances without the marriage bond than within it. These are some of the revolutionary and sensational teachings submitted with academic warrant to the minds of hundreds of thousands of students in the United States.
Such, then, is the teaching imbibed by youth at its most susceptible stage; can we wonder that these theories obtain large circulation and that high honour and enthusiastic support await those so-called "daring spirits" who rail at convention and scoff at morality?
But it is not necessary to wander so far afield. Our own public schools of Ontario are not so entirely spotless that we should accept similar institutions without the most searching inquiry. I quote from an article

which recently appeared in a well-known newspaper. It is entitled "Depravity in Canadian Schools," and reads:
Declaring our public schools were nurseries for budding criminals, Dr. C. K.
