The Polish language was proscribed, yet to-day the Parliament of Canada guarantees by solemn treaty that never again will it be interfered with. The Irish, robbed of their native Gaelic, have learned to express their loathing of the oppressor in the classical language of Milton and Shakespeare. To deprive the French-Canadians of their rights guaranteed by treaty and sanctified by tradition would be a repudiation of the most sacred obligations of the British Crown. But with that reservation it seeme to us that the existence of two languages in the Dominion, and their encouragement by teaching in the schools, should be a source of strength and not of weakness. Other considerations of no less importance occur to us in studying this question. The expense connected with the organization of a national system or even of an innocuous Board could hardly be justified. The present disastrous state of our finances does not permit us to indulge in the luxury of costly useless experiments.
The disorganization involved in the destruction of an old system and the inauguration of a new one would in all probability deprive the children of one or two generations of the benefits of any education whatever, and we must all admit that it is within the next few years that Canada's greatest trial is to come and unless our people are prepared to face the future strong in the sanity of our growing generation we may expect to be defeated in the struggle.
Without attempting to pose either as a great historian or as a constitutional authority, I am convinced that without section 93 of the British North America Act-that dealing with education-the Confederation pact would never have been entered into and that its violation would be equivalent to the denunciation of the whole bargain to such an extent that any of the parties thereto could and should consider themselves free to return to their original status. Such a rupture is unthinkable and could not but entail the most disastrous consequences.
I wish to treat this subject from the standpoint of Canada as a whole, and it is with that end in view that I ask that this resolution be not pressed, that the House be not divided. I have stated some of our reasons for opposing even the slightest encroachment on our rights. Suffice it to say that we hold our autonomy in educational matters as a thing sacred and. beyond recall. We cannot agree to relax one jot, to change one comma of our Magna Charta. Surely the hon. gentleman does not desire to open once more in this country the floodgates of racial and religious strife, to make us a prey to the devastating flame of sectional intolerance. We give him credit for the honesty of his convictions; let him respect ours. We desire nothing except to be left alone. Cannot he find in this country of ours other spheres of activity, other conditions more in need of his reforming zeal? Let him remember that we on this side of the House are his countrymen. In fact the name which he so proudly attributes to himself to-day, that of Canadian, -was first applied as a term almost of derision by his ancestors to the forefathers of a number of gentlemen now sitting around me. I, too, am a Canadian, simple and unhyphenated. My affections are centred in this land and I neither owe nor own allegiance to any other country. I am not even a French-Canadian, though I may say in passing that the kindly treatment meted out by. a generous people to my exiled forefathers and generations of their descendants have led me to sympathize with my fellow-citizens of French descent in their struggle to keep their national status intact to such an extent that my best energies will always be devoted to that end. It is because I am a Canadian and because I have a passionate belief, almost sublime faith in our future destiny, that I take this matter so much to heart. To my mind anything which interferes with the development of national unity and the propagation of broad, true Canadianism is a national crime. Our hopes are too high, our future too bright, our manifest destiny too great, for us at this date by our own action to place them in jeopardy.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want this important debate to close without rising in my place in order to protest against the resolution moved by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards).

It occurs to me that, whenever referring to educational matters before this Parliament, every hon. member should be actuated by that sincerity which every Canadian should possess who respects the constitution and is anxious about the progress which has been achieved in educational matters throughout the provinces.
I oppose the resolution moved by the hon. gentleman, on two grounds.
The school system based upon a federal bureau of education is unconstitutional, and further more it involves a useless overlapping of work. First, that educational system is unconstitutional. The hon. member for Frontenac-if I may so sum up his view, told us: there will be introduced into the federal sphere an educational system, to the end that a common patriotic ideal may 'be instilled in the minds of our younger generation. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that I am doing no injustice to the gentleman in placing on such high ground the debate liaised by his resolution. On the other hand, the constitution of the country tells us that the. provinces have exclusive jurisdiction over matters of education within their boundaries, and in order to achieve that result and effectively control education, they have the power of enforcing their own. ideal, that is to say, the various provinces are given by the constitution control over educational matters, in accordance with their respective ideals.
Undoubtedly, what the hon. gentleman is aiming at, is to introduce a system which would be inconsistent and conflicting with a state of thing that is prevailing beyond any question throughout the country. Therefore, the educational system that he wants to establish is unconstitutional and that is why I view it with fear and alarm. Should he tell us: I am going to ask for an amendment to the constitution in order to enable us to introduce that system, I would still say: Hands off! Do not interfere with the constitution. In a similar sphere, among the most important and sacred duties which devolve upon the provinces, education is certainly to be found. We have already made so many attempts against the -constitution of this country, and that in so many ways and under so many pretences, that it is high time we did discountenance all such attacks against the spirit of the constitution.
Furthermore, I say that such an educational system as advocated by the hon. member for Frontenac is a useless duplicating of work.

In order to bring about educational progress, there must of necessity exist a public organization and it is of the highest importance that such an organization be headed by experienced educationalists, by competent men, devoted to the cause of education, and I submit that we already have such a mechanism, making for the progress of education. In fact, each province possesses its own department of education, while the ability and devotedness ,of its higher officials are duly appreciated, commended and applauded by everybody. Does the hon. gentleman believe that the officials of this central bureau of education would better discharge their duties than the officials of the provincial departments are now doing? Therefore, seeing that these provincial departments answer the purpose very well, it follows that a federal bureau would he a useless duplicating of work, and should even say, a harmful mechanism.
In law-making, everything superfluous should be eliminated. Therefore it is idle for us to enact laws which admittedly will prove superfluous or inefficient. We should bend our efforts towards enacting really progressive and wise laws.
Now, I shall content myself with, making reference to another matter that is essentially involved in the hon. gentleman's proposition and that is in connection with the ideal which the hon. member for Frontenac dreams of instilling in the minds of the children of this country.
What is the school ideal advocated by the honourable member for Frontenac? I easily fancy what it is, and I am obliged to solemly declare that, in my estimation^ if the brains of the children of this country were moulded on such an ideal, it would be a misfortune for the whole Dominion. It

seems to me, moreover, that th:-s resolution is submitted to Parliament at a most inopportune time. Such a public rebuke to the devoted servants of the school in every province of the Dominion in spite of the federal constitution and of the progress realized, is most untimely at this very hour when the progress achieved by every province in the sphere of education is admitted on all sides; when we see, with such a great satisfaction and I would even say with such a jealous pride, the forward .movement of education in all the provinces and more especially in the province of Quebec; when we see, as we do to-day, a whole people in the act of offering a tribute of public admiration and of gratitude to the pioneer of popular education who was Marguerite Bourgeois, and to her beneficdent and incomparable 'Congregation.

Mr. Speaker, during the not inconsiderable number of years that I have had the honour of being a colleague of my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) in this House I have admired the assiduity and the hard work which he puts into his duties; and I am bound to say that I think he has done a national service to-day by the speech in which he introduced the proposal of his resolution. Nobody could find the slightest fault with the spirit of his speech; it was couched from end to end in tolerant language and was characterized by a moderate tone; and certainly no one could find the slightest fault with the object which he clearly told us he had in view, that of promoting the national unity of Canada. I apprehend that that is an object that ought to be dear to the heart of every Canadian. There is no getting away from the fact that, young as we are in history as a country, we suffer a very great deal from what I venture to define as narrow provincialism, and the promotion of national unity as the object of any hon. member of this House in supporting any proposition is surely a duty which might well devolve upon this, the national Parliament of Canada.
Now, with regard to the merits of the proposal which the hon. member has brought before the House, I am bound to say that on broad and general grounds I find myself in agreement with it. It was to be expected, of course, that the constitutional question would at once be raised. It was raised by my hon. friend from Beauce (Mr. Boland) and more emphatically and more exclusively by my hon. friend from East Quebec (Mr. Lapointe). No one in
this House has greater admiration for the qualities of my hon. friend from East Quebec than I have. I have frequently had occasion to admire his logic. But on this question of constitutionality, Mr. Speaker,
I am bound to say that my hon. friend's logic halted considerably in the short address which he made to us to-night. When it was a question of carrying the proposal of my hon. friend's resolution, he said: I stand upon the constitution of the country; that constitution is to be found in the British North America Act; there I stand, within the four corners of that Act, and nothing can move me along the lines of any sympathy whatsoever with the resolution of my hon. friend from Frontenac. But in the same breath he said, what w'e all know: That almost from the moment of Confederation when it suited other purposes of hon. gentlemen in various parties in this House, they have without a moment's hesitation driven a carriage and pair through the constitution. He told us in so many words that there were certain interferences with the constitution that he would at once accede to. He said he did not propose to be going forever across the Atlantic to get the permission of the Imperial Parliament to superannuate a judge. With that point of view I am in absolute sympathy. But if that be good practice in the matter of the superannuation of a judge, then I turn to my hon. friend from East Quebec, who, I am sorry to note, is absent from his seat for the moment, with the question which he put to the member for Frontenac: If you are going to interfere with the constitution on your lines, where are you going to stop? I think 1 am quite logical when I turn to my hon. friend from East Quebec and say that this question comes very well to him. My hon. friend's logic, therefore, halted very considerably.
On the general question of the British North America Act, T apprehend that that Act, passed as it was by the Imperial Parliament, including the House of Lords, of fifty years ago-who were no wiser than they should have been, lords though they were-I apprehend that that Act will not remain as the sole guide of Canadians for all time.
I venture that prophecy. As a matter of fact, history bears me out. I repeat that we have again and again driven a carriage and pair through the British North America Act; and I agree with the general and broad proposition of my hon. friend from East Quebec when he says that this country will

in time make its own constitution. That is good Canadian nationality, and it does not interfere with my being a good Imperialist, as I understand Imperialism, of a sane and moderate order.
I cannot see how any reasonable hon. gentleman in this House can take very much exception to the objects of the bureau as my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) defined them. It is true he did not go into any great detail as to what would be the functions of the board which in his resolution he proposes to establish. But he did mention some things. He said that it might be possible for such a board to collect information for the purpose of instructing the inhabitants of the various provinces of Canada with regard to the work of the different educational institutions in those provinces. What possible exception could there be to a board for collecting information? How could that possibly interfere with the rights of the provinces, or make for anything but the better instruction of our citizens throughout the whole of this wide Dominion in what is going on in the matter of education in the various parts of the country? How could it do anything but make for what, my hon. friend says is its object, the promotion of national unity, by perfectly innocent, harmless and broad courses of procedure? Fortunately to-day he made what, to my mind, was a wholly admirable speech because he, for the time being forgot one-tenth of himself. I repeat that in the objects of the board as he defined them I could find no objection whatsoever; and I say on my own account that this board could do very good work by way of suggestion along certain lines of common education

great nation, and we shall; we are a great nation now, and we shall become a vastly greater one-'we must remember, in Quebec, or in Ontario, or in the West, that we are still infants nationally. My hon. friend from East Quebec, whom I am glad now to see in his place, said that there are different races and creeds in Canada. Well, we are all painfully aware of that fact. We are painfully aware of the fact that there are different races and creeds in the British -Isles; they scrap a good deal over there in regard to matters that divide us in this country. Of course we have different races and creeds in Canada. Does mv hon. friend think that the exact degree of approach between the races and creeds in Canada has been reached for all time at the present moment? Surely not. Why, the history of France and the history of Britain, show that in each of these countries the nation was compounded originally, hundreds and hundreds of years ago, of men who differed as much in race and creed as the various peoples who compose Canada do to-day. And the same is true of every great nation in Europe. But I find that:
-through the ages one increasing purpose runs,
And the thoughts of men are widened with the process of the suns.
And if I wanted for a moment to assume the role of prophet, I am just as confident as I can be that, as revealed in the histories of these nations, the process of time will merge the races in this country to a far greater degree than they are merged at the present time, that creeds will modify and, as I say, our thoughts will "widen with the process of the suns."
My hon. friend from Beauce (Mr. Beland) made a very clean-cut distinction between education and what he called "instruction."
I am not so sure that he was sound in the position he took on that subject. He defined instruction as the mere imparting of information to the mind of man, while he defined education as the development of the qualities of the heart. Well, I am quite sure that in his language he was not physiologically accurate. The heart is a hollow muscle whose duty it is to take the blood through the various parts of the corporeal frame of man; and the qualities of the heart, as he used the word, are to my way of thinking, equally with the qualities of intellect, the constituent parts of the mind.
I apprehend that in his teaching he minimized the importance of the influence of instruction upon the moral nature as well as the intellectual nature of the child growing into the man. I am old enough

to remember when the first compulsory education Act w-as instroduced in Great Britain, and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members of this House, that the statistics as to juvenile crime in Britain as a result of that Act were perfectly amazing in their nature. The effect of the education of children along the lines of secular instruction, and the storage of the mind, combined, of course, with the control which every child undergoes when it attends school, produced a tremendous diminution in the juvenile crime in the Old Country. So that I do not quite go the length of my hon. friend in his distinction between instruction and education, between the qualities of mind and the qualities of heart. I should like to guard myself at this point against any possible misunderstanding by saying that all the hon. member said about the importance of the development of the moral nature, all that he said about the importance of the qualities of heart, the instilling of religion as opposed to the mere teaching of intellect, had my fullest and warmest approbation; and there is no man in this House who does not believe, with all the firmness of conviction that is possible to a man, in the great work which is being done in this country at the present time for stabilizing the opinion and conduct of the people in the disturbed condition of the world by the religious education that is given in the province of Quebec. But my hon. friend from Frontenac expressly guarded himself against any expression upon that point. He was most emphatic in his declaration that he did not want to interfere in any degree whatsoever with provincial rights. But he expressed the belief that this board might be useful along these various lines. Why should it not be possible by way of suggestion to give us some common ground of history that might be taught in all the provinces of Canada? What possible harm could come from that? I remember well that in an address Mr. Morley gave, when he was quite a young man, to the Institute of Education in Birmingham, on popular culture, he made an eloquent plea for the study of universal history. He said he was rather amazed in a recent visit to America to find that the people of that great country seemed to date history from the year 1776, and he added that there were some important happenings in the world before that date. I think we would all agree with the statement of that philosophic educationalist and statesman who is still left as one of the great ornaments of the British Empire. Yet I would say, sir, that there were important happenings in
this world before the year '67, and that there are lines of instruction that might be suggested for every province in Canada, which would not interfere with provincial rights, that would see to it that every child in every province would get at least these' fundamentals and that in that way he was being trained up to be a good citizen not of a province but of a country, or, for that matter, not of a country but of an empire and not of an empire but of a world.
I do not know that it would be impossible to make suggestions even along the lines of a common education in morals or in reli-. gion if you like. Why should not such a suggestion to every province of the Dominion take the form that it would be a good thing for every child growing up in Canada to know that Queen Victoria, wdien asked what was the source of England's greatness, said it was the Bible; or that Thomas Carlyle, when he addressed the students as rector of Glasgow University, said that no country that divorced itself from belief in a Divine Being ever attained or, at any rate retained, greatness? Why should it not be possible for every child that grew up in Canada to be taught that Emerson said that the great ages of the world have been the ages of belief? I would suggest to hon. gentlemen that along all these lines it would be quite possible for a bureau, such as my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) proposes, to throw out suggestions that would be useful in every province in the Dominion.
For these reasons, if there were nothing but, the constitutional question, I should, if this mbtion went to a division, vote unhesitatingly with the hon. member for Frontenac. I did not notice that the hon. member for East Quebec (Mr. Lapointe) or the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) were at all successful in dealing with the precedent of the United States. I labour under the difficulty of not knowing the exact educational status of the United States. I do not know how far the rights of the state in the United States are similar in matters of education to the rights of the province in this country, but I should rather think that the hon. member for Frontenac could possibly give us some information on that question indicating that education in the United States is as much a state prerogative as education in a province is a provincial prerogative in Canada. If that be so-and T notice that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Edwards-nods his approval-then surely we ought to give consideration to the fact by looking at this question on its merits, remembering that such a bureau as is proposed has actually

existed in the United States for fifty years, has existed without infringing state rights and on the whole has made for national unity. On that point I must- say that I think my hon. friend's argument was entirely sound and strong.
There is a further word, Sir, that I want to say-a word which I have no doubt the right hon. the leader of the House (Sir George Foster) will say when his time to speak-if he does speak on this subject-arrives; there is the financial question before Canada at the present time as well as the constitutional question. As some hon. gentlemen have indicated this proposition, if it [DOT] were pushed in some quarters, would evidently lead to strong ebullitions of religious and racial prejudices. I cannot say that I was very much impressed with my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power) who made the speech of a young man. If, of course, my hon. friend from Frontenac had it in his mind to create a board which would produce a large number of unmarried mothers of thirteen years of age and would storm the Eock of Ages, I should be very strongly opposed to the board; but from the very mild and almost lamblike speech of the hon. member for Frontenac I did not really gather that he had any such object in view. However, I repeat, the very fact that such an extract should be read in this House indicates that the pushing of this question at this time might give us an exhibition of race narrowness and creed intolerance that would not come from Ontario. The best evidence of it is to be found in the speech and the quotations that it contained.
I return however to the financial question. I apprehend the Government has not many millions that it is looking for avenues to shoot them into at the present moment. I take it that the Government have more holes for dollars than they have dollars for holes; and as the question, if pushed unduly, and if money were spent on this movement at this time, would give rise to a great deal of factious contention, I think that probably for the moment my hon. friend has served an excellent purpose by raising what has been one of the most interesting discussions that I have ever listened to on a private member's day in this House. We have all got something to think about, we have all learned something in the debate, and it may be wise for the hon. gentleman not to press his resolution at this time. But if it Is pressed as being something more than an academic motion moved on a private member's day, for the reasons

that I have stated I shall vote with the hon. member for Frontenac.

Mr. Speaker, on the 7th Miay last year there was introduced into the Senate this resolution:
That there should toe established in Canada a National Free Compulsory School System.
That resolution was debated, and withdrawn after ample evidence had been given that the honourable gentlemen of the Senate were not in favour of the proposal. Seven days later, on the 14th of May, my hon. friend from Frontenac, speaking to a resolution which had been placed by him on the Order Paper, made the following observations in a motion to go into Committee of Supply:
Early in the session I placed the following resolution on the Order Paper:
" That, in the opinion of this House, it is desirable that the British North America Act should be amended so as to secure the establishment of a non-sectarian school system throughout the Dominion of Canada."
A careful perusal of the hon. gentleman's speech on that occasion leads one to the conclusion that he, at least at that time, would have been willing to have the British North America Act amended so as to bring about his desire for national schools.

May I tell my hon.
friend?-I am still willing.

I notice that my hon. friend is still firm in the belief, in presenting his speech to-day, he was very careful more than once to say that he had no desire to infringe upon provincial rights. I am sure we all agree with the sentiments expressed by the hon. gentleman in his desire for national unity and in his wish not to interfere with provincial rights. I prefer, however, to take the evidence contained in his speech rather than the statement he has just made, because my hon. friend must acknowledge that if he follows out the details, as enunciated in his resolution of last year, his policy will involve an interfer-ance with provincial rights.

May I point out to
my hon. friend that my resolution of last year is not on all fours with the present resolution, and has nothing whatever to do with it. I made that perfectly clear.
I was just emphatic in regard to this resolution as I was last year in regard to the other-they are along entirely different lines.

Well my hon. friend does
not seem to be quite clear as to his own position. However, I am not going to pursue that feature of the question. I have not had the advantage of a legal training, and I am not going to discuss the constitutional feature which is involved in this debate. In the argument presented by my hon. friend he drew particular attention to the conditions in the United States. I notice that he did not go to Great Britain for a precedent. In 1909, my hon. friend who is now the Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) introduced into Parliament a resolution in favour of technical education which led to a very interesting and instructive debate. As a result of that debate the Minister of Labour of that day-my hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) who is now the leader on this side-communicated with the Prime Ministers of the different pr; [DOT] vinces of Canada asking if they had any objection to the Federal Government sending a commission to study the question of technical education. In the report of the commission, appointed at that time, hon. gentlemen will find the replies of the premiers of the nine Canadian provinces. Three of those prime ministers most emphatically, but courteously, intimated to the then Minister of Labour that they had no objection whatever to the proposal providing it did not interefere with provincial rights. One of the three prime ministers at that time who was careful to state that he stood for provincial rights in the matter was the Prime Minister of Ontario, the late Sir James Whitney. Another prime minister who was also careful to state the position of his Government upon that question was the Prime Minister of Manitoba, Sir Rodmand Roblin. The third Prime Minister was Sir Lomer Gouin, then and now the Premier of the province of Quebec. So that the prime ministers of three of the great provinces of this Dominion carefully placed before the Federal Government at that time their position as regards the matter of education. But there is another authority of more recent date whom we can quote to-day as being strong for provincial rights in respect to matters of education. Only a few days ago in this Chamber there was a debate in which the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) took part, and we find the hon. gentleman making use of these observations as reported on page 865 of Hansard:
The task of Canadianizing the foreign-born is fundamentally and solely a question of education. The provinces, under the Canadian Constitution, have jurisdiction in matters of education. Not only have they jurisdiction, hut their authority is exclusive on that subject-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must remind the hon. gentleman that he is not in order in quoting from a previous debate in the same session.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker. Now let us follow the commission on technical education, of which Dr. James W. Robertson was the Chairman. Hon. gentlemen who are interested in matters of education could not do better than carefully study the most interesting and instructive report published by that commission. I am only going to deal with a few sentences from it, but I wish more particularly to point out, especially to my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) this fact. We find in that report the statement-made that England and Scotland had a common school department for elementary education in 1837; but in 1866, to meet the desire of the Scottish people to improve the educational system of Scotland, that country separted from England in this matter and received her grant from the Exchequer for Scottish education. So it was with Ireland. Ireland was not satisfied to be dictated to from London as to her system of education, and so to-day they have in the British Isles a system of education for England and Wales-and Wales has its owrn separate department-a system for Scotland, and a system for Ireland. Now what was the condition at the time when the British Isles had one system of education? I have under my hand an editorial from the St. Johns News, and by the way that paper is a loyal and faithful supporter of the old Conservative party, and has been for many years. If I am not mistaken, it is controlled by the hon. member for St. Antoine division of Montreal Sir Herbert Ames). I find in the editorial referred to this statement:
Years ago many illiterates came to Canada from rural England, but the percentage is very small to-day. In 1843, over 40 per cent of the men and women who were married in England that year had to sign the parish registers with a cross. In 1907 the percentage had fallen to less than 2 per cent.
So we see that under that central system eduoation is very defective in the British Isles, but when the system was decentralized, so that England, Scotland, Ireland and Wales each had its own separate system, education improved by leaps and bounds until to-day their systems are excellent. I argue from this experience that we will be better advised to leave well

enough alone and continue a system which, I grant you, is possibly not altogether satisfactory to the people of the whole Dominion, but it will be a bad thing for all the provinces when we are absolutely satisfied with our educational systems.
I submit that any improvement we may find desirable can be brought about better by local initiative than by a central authority here in Ottawa, I ask the people of British Columbia, for instance, would they be better satisfied with the administration of their schools from Ottawa instead of from Victoria? If there were abuses to be remedied, could the remedy be applied easier from Ottawa than from Victoria? I ask the people of Alberta, could they handle their educational problems better from Ottawa than from Edmonton? And so with the. people of Nova Scotia-would they be better satisfied if their excellent system of education was scrapped and they were dictated to by Ottawa in their school affairs?
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, having this in mind, I join in the appeal of my hon. friend from Bed Deer (Mr. Clark) to my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) who is so desirous of promoting national unity, to withdraw this resolution, which at this time can do no good and, in my judgment, may do some harm.

speakeroldname: Et. Hon. Sir GEOEGE FOSTEE (Acting Prime Minister):
speechtext:
I do not rise, Mr. Speaker, for the purpose of debating at any length the question which has been discussed in a very temperate and, I think, in many respects a very able way. I rise, because the resolution as worded is an instruction for immediate activity on the part of the Government, involving both organization and expense, and I want to say a word or two upon that side of the question. But before doing so I might be permitted to say something with reference to the general trend of the discussion. I think we will all agree that the final word on educational systems has not yet been spoken. I think it is fair to say that there is probably a tenser interest and a more persistent and intensive inquiry into past systems of education and into the results that have come from them than probably at any other period in the history of our country, and maybe I am right in extending that to the history of other countries as w'ell. We have not reached finality in regard to system, theory, or practice. I think we are making great progress towards that end and I think we ought to be well satisfied in a way with past progress, with-
IMi, Robb.]
out thereby becoming indifferent as to progressive methods for the betterment of present practice, because betterment is always possible and we must always strive for it, or we will become indifferent, lax, and ineffective in our educational methods and attainments.
I listened carefully to the discussion initiated by my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), and I really failed to discover any attack on provincial rights. I really did understand all through the discussion as he conducted it and as it was continued by most of the other speakers, that there was a sedulous desire to avoid interference with provincial rights, and rather a seeking to know whether or not, keeping provincial rights intact, a possible betterment might not result from the establishment of some agency which would be consultative and co-operative in its nature, making for uniformity where it would be for the benefit of the nation, and preventing duplication where it would be against the general educational advancement of the whole country. I took that to be the spirit of the initiator of the discussion this afternoon.
I am not sure whether the establishment of such an agency w'hich, proceeding from the provinces themselves, in that general line of progress by evolution, by consultation, by union meetings of educational authorities from all the provinces, by a gradual throwing into a general treasury of thought and of exchange the best experience of every province in its educational system, might not lead to the evolution of improved educational systems in ail the provinces. It is not impossible that that oould be brought about from above, and that we could form a bureau in connection with the federal authority which would do a lot of that informative and cooperative work towards uniformity and betterment.
There is room for two different schools of thought, and each school may be absolutely honest and straightforward in its convictions and in the way it puts those convictions before the other. We must not quarrel because we may have two schools of opinion. There ought to be such a spirit in this forum that any man can honestly and straightforwardly express his opinions for the benefit and advancement, of the country without being charged or taunted with making mischief or desiring to usurp provincial rights. We cannot be the deliberative forum we ought to be unless we have charity, generosity, and good sense

enough to grant to every one the statement of his opinions as well as the possession of his convictions. And so, although I may not agree altogether with much that was said, for instance, by my hpn. friend from Quebec, yet those are his convictions: with some of his views I did agree, and I take what is suggestive and helpful to me; and he may get something helpful from me or from another member who expresses a different view. Again I put my plea forward, -do not let us see, in what is honestly striven for and spoken, attacks either on provincial systems of education or on provincial rights in any other respect.
Now, surely there are respects in which there is no difference between the educationalist from Quebec and the educationalist from Nova Scotia and the educationalist from any other of our provinces. So that a bureau established on right lines, in accordance with the higher general ideas of educational thought among the provinces, a bureau of help and a suggestion and information, might be a great aid in the educational progress and development of the country.
There are difficulties in the way. The first would be the question: what amount of 'authority shall that bureau have? It must not be a fancy 'thing; if you go to the expense and trouble of organizing it you want to have a thing which is virile, a thing which had strength. If it is simply a name and a label, we are far better without it, because it would do no good and might do a great deal of mischief. So that if such a bureau is to be effective, it must have well-defined duties. In defining those duties great care would be required. I do not think it is possible to define them without close consultation with the educational authorities of the different provinces, so that there would be common consent with regard to what those duties should be. If the proposal were that the bureau should act in a directive capacity as regards education in the different provinces, it would not be workable. It would not be accepted by the provinces now, nor do 1 know when it would be. Clearly, therefore, some limits would have to be recog nized in the creation of any such organization. In the long years of the past we have constantly come closer together in all the higher and greater lines of our thought and action, and I believe that in the future we shall continue to grow closer together, to have more in common, to work collectively and co-operatively even to a greater extent than we have worked in the past. So
it may be that after careful thought we may be able to get that help, either coming from this federal body, or, as I would rather see it come, as the evolution of a gradual progress and development in educational matters in the different provinces. It would be a benefit to have something which would make for uniformity in the great spiritual, moral and intellectual lines followed by our educational systems. We need stimulus and interest. Prince Edward Island is but a small flick in the ocean. It has a hundred thousand people; it has its educational system. But do you mean to say that a small province like that would not benefit so far as its educational system is concerned through the inspiration of other and larger systems of education in the other provinces? So with all the provinces. I do not think we have got to the last word in the matter of educational organization in any of the provinces; noi have we got to the last word in out educational system in this country as a whole. But we shall come to it by gradual processes, whether from the outside towards the centre, or from the centre towards the outside. And we must be a bit patient. We have had a fair discussion of the subject to-day. Others than those who spoke in favour of the resolution this afternoon feel that more ought to be done than has been done with reference to our general educational system, arid who are looking to some such method as has been suggested to bring about co-relation and co-operation in our general life of uplift, intellectual and moral.
Having thus in a brotherly way, in an honest and temperate way, interchanged oui views on this matter, we may allow these things to be further discussed and thought over. Every .year we shall probably hear more about this education ques-
10 p.m. tion. There are grades of education. The idea of education which was in the minds of the fathers of Confederation was probably different from that which prevails now. The idea of education broadens. To-day there is not much difference of opinion along certain lines of intellectual and moral uplift, and ias to the way these may be carried on through the federal authority without impinging in the least upon the rights of the provinces. But what I particularly desire to say is that if this resolution passes to-night it is a direction that we shall do something which is at the present moment indefinite. However well the mover of the resolution has explained What he meant by it, the pro-



posal is-I was going to say, .without form and void; at least it is indefinite. Who is to interpret what the proposed body shall be? What is it that is to be formed? On this indefinite basis we can hardly receive a direct instruction to set up an organization and to put something into force. Further, I should not like to see anything of this kind done unless it is well organized, well thought out, is strong and capable of bringing to effect the purpose for which it was intended. That requires money; that requires financial assistance, and financial assistance is to be looked at very carefully by a government which is administering the affairs of the country under the peculiar conditions which exist to-day. So that on both those counts which I have mentioned, and need not mention again, I would deprecate that a direct instruction should be given to the .Government to carry out, with all the organization and financial backing which it implies a resolution suc'h as my hon. friend has moved.
I am free to say that I am not sorry that this discussion has taken place in this Parliament. T think it is infinitely better than a discussion the whole purpose of which is for one of us to try and rag another one of us, for one side of the House to have a heated party discussion with the other side. It is a kind of a cooler atmosphere we get into if we can take a resolution, somewhat academic but which has real substance in it, and discuss it as men and gentlemen on both sides of the House and as representatives of the people's needs end requirements.
My hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) has moved his resolution, and has supported it and we have had a certain discussion upon it. I am not his dictator, and I am not going to say to him whether I think he ought to withdraw it or not. But I do wish to say to him that the Government does not like to take an instruction, so positive as this, in the words of his resolution at this time. He might consider it better to withdraw his resolution, or it might be disposed of in some other way. I congratulate him for my part, and I have no disposition to do otherwise, upon provoking, or rather leading up to a discussion which I think will have no bad results, and which has certainly done something with reference to opening up questions which will be more discussed both in and out of this House before they are' less discussed.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. L. DAVIDSON (Digby and Annapolis):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I .beg leave to move the adjournment of the debate.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is there a seconder' for the motion?
Mr. EDWARDS': The right hon. Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster) has pretty clearly intimated to me and to the members at least on this side of the House that should I decide to let this resolution go to a vote, supporters of the Government would be expected to vote it down. He said it might be disposed of by withdrawal or in some other way, and I suppose that that is what he meant by "some other way." I want to assure the Acting Prime Minister that so far as the voting down of my resolution is concerned, I would not have any hesitation in submitting it even if I were the only one to stand up and vote for it. The intimation that it was to be voted down would have no effect on me whatever.
The Acting Prime Minister has objected to this resolution from the standpoint of its indefiniteness. Now I was rather under the impression that the very fact of its indefiniteness would appeal to members of the Government. Why? .Because just three weeks ago to-day a resolution was moved in this House by the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) in regard to the educating or Canadianizing of the foreign element in this country, and though that resolution was very indefinite it was accepted not only by the Government but by every member of this House, and agreed to unanimously. iSo it was good policy three weeks ago to move an indefinite resolution, which was accepted, but it is bad policy to-day to move a resolution which has in it elements of indefiniteness. At the beginning of my remarks this afternoon I called attention to the resolution which was moved by the hon. member for South Perth and adopted, and I pointed out that that resolution most distinctly stated that the national welfare of Canada made it imperative that appropriate measures should be taken by this Parliament to fit and prepare the alien in this country to exercise the functions of citizenship. There was a clear acknowledgment that he was not now fit to exercise these functions, and a clear acceptance of the indefinite proposition that "appropriate measures" should be taken. Yes, the House agreed, and the Government agreed, that these aliens are not as they should be. Yes, we agreed that "appropriate measures should be taken" to

educate and fit them to perform their duties as Canadian citizens, but there was no statement as to what those "appropriate measures" should be. The resolution was so beautifully indefinite that it could be readily accepted by the Government and by every lion, member of this House.
The proposition which I have submitted to the House for a Federal Bureau of Education leaves the door wide open. I might say in all frankness and candour that I did not expect the Government would be able to take hold of this matter after only a Cabinet consultation, for instance, and arrive at any proper conclusion as to what should be done. Therefore, I suggested as the first step to be taken by this Government that they should invite the several provinces to send educationalists to Ottawa to consult witn the Government and devise or suggest a mode of procedure by which this Bureau of Education might be inaugurated.
We have, however, had a pretty definite admission from hon. gentlemen in this House this afternoon that conditions in this country are not as they should be, that there is room for improvement, that something might be done along co-operative lines. I can read in those remarks of the Acting Prime Minister and of other hon. gentlemen who have spoken, that in the back of their heads they really believe in this principle of a bureau, whether you call it a Federal Bureau or not. They believe in the principle of having a Bureau of Education that will be a sort of clearing-house for the gathering and dissemination of ideas throughout the country.
Of course, we have an apprehension on the part of some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, and 1 wish for a moment to refer to some of the things that have been said by certain of these hon. gentlemen. I have no fault to find with the position taken by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland)-. While he indicated that he had some apprehension of an invasion of provincial rights if this bureau were established, yet in presenting his remarks his language, as always, was courteous and gentlemanly.
But I suppose I could not very well expect the example set by the hon. member for Beauce to be followed by all those who spoke on the other side. I was struck with this fact, as I am sure you must have been, Mr. Speaker, if you followed the discussion -and hon. gentlemen who have had the advantage of legal training would of course observe it more readily than a layman like
myself, although I could not help noticing it-that the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), expressed respect for my convictions while the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) said something to the same effect. They professed to give me credit for honesty of conviction. But *while these two gentlemen paraded their confidence in me and the honesty of my convictions, they were the only two who proceeded in the course of their remarks to charge me with political crookedness in the introduction of this resolution. They both said that I had made a frontal attack last year in the resolution I introduced on that occasion, and that I was coming back by a flank attack in introducing this resolution to-day. The hon. member for Quebec South particularly said that I was assailing, or at least endeavouring to get at, the province of Quebec in this resolution. He stated that I had travelled over the prairies in order to arrive at Quebec and, by a flank movement, to have a chance of attacking that province; and the hon. member for Quebec East, referring to the resolution which I moved last year, showed the sincerity of the "confidence" which he said he had in the honesty of my convictions by at once indicating his suspicion of my motives in the previous resolution and that which I moved this afternoon. He -asked: Why should he come back with a resolution which he knows cannot be accepted-what purpose has the hon. gentleman to serve? Well, may I ask the hon. member for Quebec East a similar question? May I ask that hon. gentleman what purpose he had to serve when, in the session of 1916, when this country was at war, and was putting forth every conceivable effort to recruit men from all parts of the Dominion, that hon. gentleman rose in his place in this House, and moved his bi-lingual resolution? What object did he hope to serve by that? What was his purpose in introducing that resolution?
-Mr. LAPOINTE: To bring peace and harmony into the country.

Yes, to bring peace and harmony into the country. But the hon. gentleman had mighty peculiar methods of bringing about that end. While that resolution was being discussed in the House on that occasion the then leader of the Opposition, the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, stated, in speaking on the matter, that he knew it wmuld bring just the opposite to harmony, namely, discord and disunity.
Never, never.
I beg to contradict my hon. friend. The right hon. gentleman did make the statement I ascribe to him.

He never did.
Mr: EDWARDS: He said we had always had a certain amount of discord and disunity, and we always would have. Now, my hon. friend attacks my motive in introducing this resolution. But I want to tell him that it comes with very poor grace from all those who sit to your left to charge me with insincerity or any other motive than that which appears on the face of the resolution. And it comes with less grace from the hon. member for Quebec East to impute ulterior motives to me, in view of the fact that the hon. gentleman moved a resolution in this House which he knew could have but one effect, and that was to. drive further apart the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. The hon. member for Quebec East, the hon. member for Quebec South, and the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb), all read into this resolution of mine what is not in it at all, and charge me with an attempt to make a flank attack on Quebec and its educational institutions. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) was good enough to say this evening that he had observed with pleasure the fact that I suppressed a part of myself in the course of my remarks. Let me say that it is very difficult for any man to maintain moderation and that tone which we should like to see prevail in debate in this House when he is followed by gentlemen who accuse him as I have been accused in this House to-day. 1 want to take this opportunity here and now to tell the hon. gentleman from Quebec East, who moved his bi-lingual resolution which meant nothing but discord and the very opposite of unity; the hon. member for Quebec South; who read a carefully prepared essay written under a wrong conception of what I was going to say when I introduced my resolution; the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon, and any other hon. gentleman from Quebec, that if you study the political history of this country from Confederation down to this very year, you will find that the only province in Confederation, from the year 1867 to this moment, that has ever interfered or presumed to interfere with the purely provincial rights of any other province, is the province of Quebec. There is not a single province in Confederation with which the province of Quebec, and members from that province, have not on the floor of the House, and throughout the country, endeavoured to interfere in their purely pro-

vincial matters. When it suits their purpose they throw to the four winds of heaven constitution and all, hut they can preach constitution, British North America Act, Section 93, and everything else, when they desire to put a wrong construction upon this motion which I present. I could give instance after instance where Quebec has interfered in matters coming solely under the constitution of Ontario. I can give instances where it has interfered with matters relating solely to the province of Manitoba, and every other province; and there is not a single instance that can be referred to where any of the other provinces since Confederation has at any time interfered with any matters coming under the jurisdiction of the province of Quebec. Yet these hon. gentlemen this afternoon, as they have done on many occasions when they desire to throw dust in the eyes of the public, come forward with an air of righteous indignation as if the rights of the province of Quebec were being infringed. There has been no attempt in this resolution to infringe the rights of any province. What is the sense of quoting the British North America Act, and Section 93 of that Act, so far as this resolution is concerned? Do hon. gentlemen suppose that I have not read that Act as well as they? Do they suppose that they are giving special information when they quote Section 93?
Mr. AROHAMiBATJLT: Yes.

I would not be surprised if my hon. friend thought he was, because he has a much higher opinion of himself than any one else holds of him. Section 93 refers to the making of law; will any one show me where in this resolution, which asks for the appointment of a Federal Bureau of Education, there is any undertaking, from first to last, to make laws in any shape or form? In what respect has this section any relevancy to the establishment of. a Federal Bureau? It is not proposed in any sense to interfere in the slightest degree with any right of any province. We could not interfere with any provincial right without going to the trouble of having our constitution changed. Do you suggest for one moment in a country of the extent of Canada the feasibility of centralizing education here at Ottawa? It is preposterous; it is utterly ridiculous. Nobody has suggested that. Nothing could have been further from my thoughts in the remarks that I have made than to suggest anything of the kind.
What was the attitude assumed by hon. gentlemen on the other side who have

spoken? These hon. gentlemen come here and assume to speak for the province of Quebec. I must take it that they are speaking for the province of Quebec. What is the attitude then of the province of <Quebee if these gentlemen are the mouthpiece for that province? We may have a 'Federal Bureau "which will act as a clearing house or, to use the words of the right hon. the Acting Prime Minister (Sir (George Foster), a treasury, into which we .can place all ideas gathered in every province of the Dominion or in every civilized country of the world, and you can, if you choose, come to that treasury, in which we have accumulated the best ideas of the civilized countries of the world along educational lines, and take what you want; you may dip into that treasury, you may help yourself if you wish to do so; or if you wish you may leave it alone. What is the attitude of hon. gentlemen, what is the attitude of the province of Quebec, that they are here as the mouthpiece for?
They are not ashamed of it.

I would have no quarrel with my hon. friends if they took this position: You may form such a treasury as that, no harm can come to any part of Canada from accumulating these ideas, but we refuse to dip into the treasury or to help ourselves to these ideas. That would be all right, but that is not the position that these hon. gentlemen take. The position they take is: We refuse to allow those provinces who wish to dip into that treasury to do so. That is the attitude of the province of Quebec and that has been the attitude of that province from Confederation down to the present time- -not only refusing to take what they want when they have a right to do it, but refusing to allow other provinces to exercise their functions in provincial and educational matters when they claimed the right to do it.
What harm could you do in a bureau established at Ottawa gathering information in regard to the school systems in the various provinces and leaving that information in a position where any province wishing to avail "itself of those accumulated ideas could do so? There is no compulsion; no province has to accept any one of these ideas unless it wants to. That has been the attitude of the United States ever since the Federal Bureau was established in that country fifty-two or fifty-three years ago. What has resulted? They have formed a bureau that has collected 90
daj,a from all over the United States and from every civilized country in regard to their educational systems. That Federal .Bureau at different times has made suggestions. It has been advisory, just as this would be advisory. Is it better to use the word "suggestive" instead of "advisory." I do not know that there is very much difference, but they have at various times made recommendations of changes which they thought it would be beneficial to make in the law of this or that state in order to improve their educational system. What happened? That was not an infringement of state rights. The states, through their educational authorities and their legislatures, decide whether the idea, or recommendation, or suggestion is a good one. If they decide it is not a good one they do not aceept it. The power to accept or reject rests entirely with the state. In *many cases suggestions or recommendations have been adopted and crystallized into legislation. That is the proposition in so far as a Federal Bureau is concerned, and it is a proposition which leaves every province absolutely free to exercise its wisdom in regard to any matter which is suggested as to whether or not it would be incorporated in the law, or whether they shall leave it alone.
How in the "world can you construe that by any possible twist of the imagination into an attack upon the rights of any province? How can yon interfere with the constitutional rights which the province has except by having that constitution changed? There is no proposal to do anything of the kind. The suggestion is made that this bureau would make a change in the law. What power would it have to make a change in the law? None whatever; its only power would be to gather information, to have, that information available for use by any person or any province that wanted to use it. If a province did not want to use it, it would not have to do so. Our friends across the way say: We will not use it and the rest of you shall not use it; if you make any attempt to accumulate the ideas which may be. valuable, which may have been found to be valuable in various parts of the world, if you make any attempt to consolidate and keep these together, we will oppose it and the charge which we will make against you is that you are attempting to drive the thin edge of the wedge into the constitution which gives to the province of Quebec its liberties. Well, Mr. Speaker, I want to say to my hon. friend? .from Quebec that if there is one province



out of the nine in Confederation which has little cause of complaint in regard to its rights and liberties, that province is Quebec. There has never been a disposition on the part of any province in the Confederation to deprive the province of Quebec at any time of any of the rights and privileges it enjoys under the constitution.
They better not try.

They better not try, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gauvreau) says. Well, I do not know. How am I to take that? How is anybody to take that? My hon. friend does not look belligerent; he is smiling at this moment. Does he intend his remark as a threat? M&ybe he intended to give point to the remark made by one of 'his colleagues from that province some days ago that the province of Quebec was waiting for its "hour." T do not know whether that is what he had in rniftd or not. I may tell my hon. friend that there is no desire to infringe the rights of the province of Quebec or any other province. I wish we could get out of the minds of hon. gentlemen in the discussion of this matter the idea that some of them seem to have-and I cannot think they are all insincere; they really have the idea- that in some shape or form this Federal Bureau will infringe on the right of the provinces to control education. Once more let me say the idea is to follow that adopted by the United States fifty-three years ago. The idea as carried out in that country is to accumulate information not only from every state in the Union but from other eoun-~ tries-Canada, England, Germany, France, and every civilized country in the world. If you want information to-day in regard to the educational system prevailing in the province of Nova Scotia or any other province you have to write to the Bureau of Education in the city of Washington to get that information. That is the position in which we are to-day. Now it has not resulted in any harm on the other side of the line where it has been in operation for 53 yeais. No person has bf'**n hurt by it, but a great deal of benefit has accrued to that country front the adoption of a Bureau of Education there. All that I ask and all that this resolution asks, is that a similar bureau be established in Ottawa which would collect imonnation, collect data, accumulate all the knowledge that we can get on mattuis of education, and would hand that information out to whatever province wanted to

make use of it. To those who do not want to make use of it no harm is done; those who would like to utilize it can do so. It we could, as my hon. friend from Red Deer-very properly it seems to 'me-said, bring some uniformity into some of our systems along, for instance, the line of history, who is hurt by it? Suppose your bureau called together educationalists, and they came to the conclusion that such and such a history would be the best to use in this country, and they recommended its adoption. Our friends from Quebec say: "No, we prefer the history which we have already." Very good, the choice rests with them to refuse or not. But if they feel, or if their education authorities consider that their history is better than the one recommended, why should they step in and deprive Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, for example, from uniting on one line of history? Why should they do it? What object have they in so _doing? Who is going to he hurt by the adoption of such a plan?
If a child starts his education in the p-o-vince of Saskatchewan and goes down to the province of Manitoba and finds that the grade there is the same as it was m Saskatchewan, or goes to Ontario and finds that the grade there is the same as it was in Manitoba, who is hurt by that? At the present time, say, the child begins his education in. Saskatchewan. In a year, perhaps, his parents take him down to Manitoba. There they find he is in grade 3, we will say, and in the Manitoba school they declared: "Yes, we will accept you in grade 3 so far as writing is concerned, but you are not up to our standard in arithmetic, and you have got to go back." And so he goes into another grade because of this difference as between Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Or perhaps, the child goes down to Quebec, where it is found he is all right in arithmetic, but probably not in his writing, and he is shifted again. What harm would be done if the educationalists of the different provinces got together and considered the systems of grading in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Ontario, and decided that so and so was the proper grading for arithmetic, for writing, and so forth? What harm would be done by such a procedure; who is hurt by it? I think it would be beneficial and would work to the best interests of the country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am not going to take up any more time in discussing this matter. I realize that there is no need of

pressing the resolution or asking hon. gentlemen to vote on it. I am going to say, Mr. Speaker, that in withdrawing the resolution, which I do with the consent of my seconder, I am doing so not because I was asked to do so by the member from Huntingdon, Quebec (Mr. Robb), because that hon. gentleman, and several other members opposite, if I am to judge by their speeches, indicated very clearly that there ought to be a Bureau of Education and instruction in this country and that it ought to be in Ottawa so that they could avail themselves of it, because they seem to be very poorly posted. I do respect, of course, the wishes of the Acting Prime Minister, and I might say, Sir, that I am influenced very strongly indeed in the conclusion I have come to by my hon. friend from Red Deer who-with his usual ability to see into a matter-appreciated apparently the object which I had in view in moving the resolution and honestly gave me credit for proper motives. I say that I am influenced very largely by his request, that he thinks under the circumstances it is better to withdraw the motion. Still, I confess to you, Mr. Speaker, I would like to see just how many members there are in this House who feel that something should be done along this line. It may be, and doubtless is, true that at the present time the Government is being pressed for money for various things in this country, and that sacrifices have to be made. Nevertheless, I want to affirm-and I say it to the members of the Government as well as to members of the House generally-that the day is coming, and it is not very far away, when there will be a Federal Bureau of Education established in this country for the collection of information and its dissemination among those who wish to avail themselves of it. I am sorry to have taken up the time of the House as long as I have, but I feel very strongly on this matter. As one who has given a part of his life-indeed, some of the best years of his life-to the profession of teaching, I have devoted some attention to educational matters, and I firmly believe that the establishment of just such a bureau would not only be of great utility to all the provinces, and of great assistance to them in perfecting and improving their educational systems, but also that it would have a tendency to break down the barriers that exist between various provinces and bring them into closer union one with the other. I ask for cooperation, not compulsion, not anything that will infringe upon provincial rights;
the whole object of this resolution is the establishment of a bureau to co-operate and work with the provinces, with the one end in view of improving our education systems and of building up in this country a citizenship that would understand their responsibilities and their duties as Canadians. Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to withdraw the resolution.
Motion withdrawn.
